While each of these 3 functions are typically managed by 3 different divisions of OEM and hence 3 different applications/systems, it is the Portal Common Component that delivers them as Integrated Experience within a unified digital retailing environment.<\/p><p>Not going in detail of every brand specific portal that exist today, a portal architecture can be abstracted as below:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 1-Abstract Portal Architecture<\/p><p>While existing Business Functions/Applications are currently accessible either through some brand specific Portal or being delivered as a standalone individual application, it is important to go through the regional IAM &amp; UAM system.<\/p><div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Portal<\/td><td>IAM<\/td><td>Centralized UAM<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Link.e.Entry<\/td><td>Identity managed in Active Directory and Portal applications are authenticated &amp; SSOed by <strong>ADFS<\/strong> (SAML)<\/td><td><strong>MyPeople<\/strong> – a centralized custom-built Roles &amp; Profiles management system<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>PSA<\/td><td>Identity managed in LDAP and applications are authenticated by either SiteMinder or <strong>Ping Federate<\/strong> (OIDC or SAML) on case-by-case basis.<br>Identity for Independent Repairer is managed in Gigya CDC (Customer Data Cloud).<\/td><td>Not Applicable; every app has its own access management<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>DealerCONNECT<\/td><td>Identity managed in LDAP and applications are authenticated by <strong>SiteMinder<\/strong> &amp; SSOed by SMSession or <strong>Ping Federate<\/strong> (SAML)<\/td><td><strong>MyPersonnel<\/strong> – a centralized custom-built Roles &amp; Profiles management system<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div>", "text": "In a very simplistic representation, a Portal is really a suite of Web-enabled applications that can be accessed by a common gateway of components such IAM (Authentication & Authorization), UAM (User Access Management – Roles & Profiles), Monitoring, Logging, Session Management, Uniform Look & Feel delivering seamless experience while a user navigates from one application to another within the Portal Boundary. \nFor e.g. Automotive vehicle sales are enhanced through integrated applications that manage vehicle inventory, incentives, and service contracts. While each of these 3 functions are typically managed by 3 different divisions of OEM and hence 3 different applications/systems, it is the Portal Common Component that delivers them as Integrated Experience within a unified digital retailing environment.\nNot going in detail of every brand specific portal that exist today, a portal architecture can be abstracted as below:\n\nFigure 1-Abstract Portal Architecture\nWhile existing Business Functions/Applications are currently accessible either through some brand specific Portal or being delivered as a standalone individual application, it is important to go through the regional IAM & UAM system.\nPortal\nIAM\nCentralized UAM\nLink.e.Entry\nIdentity managed in Active Directory and Portal applications are authenticated & SSOed by ADFS (SAML)\nMyPeople – a centralized custom-built Roles & Profiles management system\nPSA\nIdentity managed in LDAP and applications are authenticated by either SiteMinder or Ping Federate (OIDC or SAML) on case-by-case basis.\nIdentity for Independent Repairer is managed in Gigya CDC (Customer Data Cloud).\nNot Applicable; every app has its own access management\nDealerCONNECT\nIdentity managed in LDAP and applications are authenticated by SiteMinder & SSOed by SMSession or Ping Federate (SAML)\nMyPersonnel – a centralized custom-built Roles & Profiles management system"}, {"id": "d2-s4", "doc": 2, "title": "Userbase for Dealer & Repairer Portal", "html": "<p>Broadly users within any organization can be classified as Internal &amp; External users. <\/p><p><strong>Internal users<\/strong> of an organization are individuals or groups who have authorized access to the organization’s internal systems, resources, and information, typically for the purpose of performing work-related tasks. These users may belong to the organization directly or have a close “contractual” working relationship with it. Such a user may also be referred to as Corporate or HQ users and may fall in following categories:<\/p><p>Business Users<\/p><p>ICT Users<\/p><p>Field Users<\/p><p><strong>External users<\/strong> of an organization are individuals or entities outside the organization’s direct structure who interact with it to access services, conduct transactions, or collaborate on business activities. While they are not employed by the organization, they often rely on its systems, platforms, or resources in structured and secure ways. Most of such users in current context would fall in following categories:<\/p><p>Dealers (Authorized/Franchised)<\/p><p>Repairers (Authorized Service Center)<\/p><p>Suppliers or Distributors<\/p><p>Independent Repairers (Business-to-Customer aka B2C)<\/p><p>Fleet Customers (Corporations, Rental Car Companies, Government Agencies etc.)<\/p><p>Following table summarizes User Type &amp; its management system to access the Stellantis IT &amp; Business Process: &lt;to-be-completed&gt;<\/p><div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Organization<\/td><td>User Category<\/td><td>ID type<\/td><td>IAM System<\/td><td>Comments<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>xF-NA<\/td><td>Business<\/td><td>TID, SFID (from Nov 2025)<\/td><td>Corporate LDAP<\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>ICT<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Field Staff<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Dealer<\/td><td>SID<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Supplier<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td>xF-EE<\/td><td>Business<\/td><td><\/td><td>Active Directory<\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>ICT<\/td><td>FID<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Dealer<\/td><td>D Code??<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td>xP<\/td><td>Business<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>ICT<\/td><td>UID, SFID<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>NSC<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Dealer<\/td><td>DN2273487<\/td><td><\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td><\/td><td>Independent Repairer<\/td><td>B2C ID<\/td><td>GIGYA CDC<\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div>", "text": "Broadly users within any organization can be classified as Internal & External users. \nInternal users of an organization are individuals or groups who have authorized access to the organization’s internal systems, resources, and information, typically for the purpose of performing work-related tasks. These users may belong to the organization directly or have a close “contractual” working relationship with it. Such a user may also be referred to as Corporate or HQ users and may fall in following categories:\nBusiness Users\nICT Users\nField Users\nExternal users of an organization are individuals or entities outside the organization’s direct structure who interact with it to access services, conduct transactions, or collaborate on business activities. While they are not employed by the organization, they often rely on its systems, platforms, or resources in structured and secure ways. Most of such users in current context would fall in following categories:\nDealers (Authorized/Franchised)\nRepairers (Authorized Service Center)\nSuppliers or Distributors\nIndependent Repairers (Business-to-Customer aka B2C)\nFleet Customers (Corporations, Rental Car Companies, Government Agencies etc.)\nFollowing table summarizes User Type & its management system to access the Stellantis IT & Business Process: <to-be-completed>\nOrganization\nUser Category\nID type\nIAM System\nComments\nxF-NA\nBusiness\nTID, SFID (from Nov 2025)\nCorporate LDAP\n\n\nICT\n\n\n\n\nField Staff\n\n\n\n\nDealer\nSID\n\n\n\nSupplier\n\n\n\nxF-EE\nBusiness\n\nActive Directory\n\n\nICT\nFID\n\n\n\nDealer\nD Code??\n\n\nxP\nBusiness\n\n\n\n\nICT\nUID, SFID\n\n\n\nNSC\n\n\n\n\nDealer\nDN2273487\n\n\n\nIndependent Repairer\nB2C ID\nGIGYA CDC\n"}, {"id": "d2-s5", "doc": 2, "title": "Platform Capabilities", "html": "<p>GDRP - a Global and Single Unified platform, is meant to be a one stop shop for all of Stellantis&#x27; Global Dealer, Repairers, HQ/Corporate/Field/Admin Users, for accessing their relevant portals and business applications as per their &#x27;User Context&#x27; (business area, role, geo, language) and &#x27;Privileges&#x27;.<\/p><p>The platform would cater to different brands from the erstwhile FCA and PSA entities as shown in the below functional architecture. The platform&#x27;s &#x27;Responsive&#x27; and &#x27;Multi-lingual&#x27; capabilities ensure that it can be accessed by users as per their &#x27;choice of language&#x27; and by &#x27;device of choice&#x27; (desktop, laptop, tablet, mobile)<\/p><p>Functionally, its &#x27;Business Capabilities&#x27; can be classified into two sub-groups viz &#x27;capabilities for the End-users&#x27; and &#x27;capabilities for the Internal Admins&#x27; (people from Stellantis Business and ICT&#x27;).<\/p><p><strong>The &#x27;End-Users&#x27;<\/strong> of the platform would be able to seamlessly login via authentication and authorization from relevant Stellantis systems, to land-up into a contextual &#x27;Landing Page&#x27; (LP – may also be referred to as Home Page) as per their &#x27;Business Area&#x27; (i.e. Sales, Aftersales, Independent Repairers and Corporate/Admin). They can access their &#x27;My Accounts&#x27; section for &#x27;Role/Dealer Toggle&#x27; within an on-going session without the need for logging-out of the platform. There is a dedicated section titled &#x27;User Profile/Preferences&#x27; for the end-user to select/change/modify the preferences for &#x27;language&#x27;, &#x27;notifications&#x27; and &#x27;the widgets displayed in the LP&#x27; <\/p><p>The users can find a contextual &#x27;Menu&#x27; at the platform header, with ability to &#x27;Bookmark&#x27; different menu items as well as would get to see the &#x27;Frequently Used Items&#x27; in the platform. For the ease of finding Menu items, user can perform a &#x27;Local Search&#x27;. At the header itself, the &#x27;Global Search&#x27; is provided to find out dynamic &#x27;Portal Content&#x27; based on &#x27;keywords&#x27; that can be &#x27;Filtered&#x27; and &#x27;Sorted&#x27; by the users.<\/p><p>Below the platform header, users can find a &#x27;Banner&#x27; depicting relevant push-communications from Stellantis via different &#x27;Knowledge Articles&#x27; in a rotating carousel. User can quickly get into the details of articles in a dedicated page for further information. They would be able to communicate and collaborate with other platform users by providing their views on the article as &#x27;Find Useful : Yes or No&#x27;, &#x27;Share Article&#x27; as links or over emails, able to &#x27;Comment on an Article&#x27; as well as &#x27;Like&#x27; someone&#x27;s already posted &#x27;Comment&#x27;<\/p><p>The LP also offers users with a quick access to different types of &#x27;Widgets&#x27; for &#x27;News, Promotions, Other Transactions&#x27; feeding into the platform from the related/relevant &#x27;Portals or Business Applications&#x27; of Stellantis as per the user-context. End-users would have the ability to change the &#x27;Ordering/Placement&#x27; of these Widgets via the &#x27;Widget Customization&#x27; feature.<\/p><p>There is a contextual &#x27;Document Repository&#x27; widget as well in the LP, that offers the users to quickly &#x27;View/Download&#x27; different digital assets uploaded by Stellantis as per the user context. A unique feature of the platform is the &#x27;Ticketing&#x27; Widget at the bottom half of the LP, where end-user would be able to quickly &#x27;View his/her own Tickets&#x27; that s/he would have created across different Stellantis &#x27;Ticketing Management Portals&#x27;<\/p><p>They would also be able to get quick support from an in-built &#x27;Chatbot&#x27; for getting answers to their &#x27;Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)&#x27;. Last but not the least is a persistent &#x27;Footer&#x27; across all pages, providing user the quick access to &#x27;FAQs&#x27;, &#x27;Privacy Policy&#x27;, &#x27;Support&#x27;, &#x27;Cookie Policy&#x27;, &#x27;Terms &amp; Conditions&#x27; and &#x27;Site Status&#x27;<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 2-GDRP Platform Capabilities<\/p>", "text": "GDRP - a Global and Single Unified platform, is meant to be a one stop shop for all of Stellantis' Global Dealer, Repairers, HQ/Corporate/Field/Admin Users, for accessing their relevant portals and business applications as per their 'User Context' (business area, role, geo, language) and 'Privileges'.\nThe platform would cater to different brands from the erstwhile FCA and PSA entities as shown in the below functional architecture. The platform's 'Responsive' and 'Multi-lingual' capabilities ensure that it can be accessed by users as per their 'choice of language' and by 'device of choice' (desktop, laptop, tablet, mobile)\nFunctionally, its 'Business Capabilities' can be classified into two sub-groups viz 'capabilities for the End-users' and 'capabilities for the Internal Admins' (people from Stellantis Business and ICT').\nThe 'End-Users' of the platform would be able to seamlessly login via authentication and authorization from relevant Stellantis systems, to land-up into a contextual 'Landing Page' (LP – may also be referred to as Home Page) as per their 'Business Area' (i.e. Sales, Aftersales, Independent Repairers and Corporate/Admin). They can access their 'My Accounts' section for 'Role/Dealer Toggle' within an on-going session without the need for logging-out of the platform. There is a dedicated section titled 'User Profile/Preferences' for the end-user to select/change/modify the preferences for 'language', 'notifications' and 'the widgets displayed in the LP' \nThe users can find a contextual 'Menu' at the platform header, with ability to 'Bookmark' different menu items as well as would get to see the 'Frequently Used Items' in the platform. For the ease of finding Menu items, user can perform a 'Local Search'. At the header itself, the 'Global Search' is provided to find out dynamic 'Portal Content' based on 'keywords' that can be 'Filtered' and 'Sorted' by the users.\nBelow the platform header, users can find a 'Banner' depicting relevant push-communications from Stellantis via different 'Knowledge Articles' in a rotating carousel. User can quickly get into the details of articles in a dedicated page for further information. They would be able to communicate and collaborate with other platform users by providing their views on the article as 'Find Useful : Yes or No', 'Share Article' as links or over emails, able to 'Comment on an Article' as well as 'Like' someone's already posted 'Comment'\nThe LP also offers users with a quick access to different types of 'Widgets' for 'News, Promotions, Other Transactions' feeding into the platform from the related/relevant 'Portals or Business Applications' of Stellantis as per the user-context. End-users would have the ability to change the 'Ordering/Placement' of these Widgets via the 'Widget Customization' feature.\nThere is a contextual 'Document Repository' widget as well in the LP, that offers the users to quickly 'View/Download' different digital assets uploaded by Stellantis as per the user context. A unique feature of the platform is the 'Ticketing' Widget at the bottom half of the LP, where end-user would be able to quickly 'View his/her own Tickets' that s/he would have created across different Stellantis 'Ticketing Management Portals'\nThey would also be able to get quick support from an in-built 'Chatbot' for getting answers to their 'Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)'. Last but not the least is a persistent 'Footer' across all pages, providing user the quick access to 'FAQs', 'Privacy Policy', 'Support', 'Cookie Policy', 'Terms & Conditions' and 'Site Status'\n\nFigure 2-GDRP Platform Capabilities"}, {"id": "d2-s6", "doc": 2, "title": "Platform Architecture in a Nutshell", "html": "<p>Before integrating any existing legacy web application or any go-to-market product-based web application or a new custom-built Greenfield web application with “The Dealer Experience” portal, it is important to understand a High-Level architecture component of the GDRP platform. The platform will evolve and mature with the ever-growing needs of the Integrating application by designing and developing reusable common component library.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 3- Platform Architecture Components<\/p><p>GDRP platform has adopted a composite architecture for its portal feature leveraging <strong>Angular<\/strong> for frontend, <strong>AWS<\/strong> for Infrastructure &amp; containerized backend microservices (BFF- Backend for Frontend) along with <strong>PaaS<\/strong> Persistent layers and SaaS Content Management Solution (CMS) from <strong>Adobe Experience Manager<\/strong>: <\/p><p>A <strong>browser as a UI (User Interface) client<\/strong> act as the <strong>front-end interface<\/strong> through which users interact with web-based portal features. It initiates OpenID Connect flow to verify a user’s identity with the Stellantis’ OIDC server a.k.a. Global Ping Fed Server.<\/p><p>Depending upon the type of User ID (described in section 1.3), Ping Federate redirects the client to regional authentication platform.<\/p><p>Dealers &amp; Authorized Repairers of xP &amp; xF-EE portals get authenticated by Active Directory (AD)<\/p><p>Internal (HQ or Corporate) users of xP &amp; xF-EE portals get authenticated either by Reunis or AD.<\/p><p>Users of xF-NA portal gets authenticated by NA Corporate LDAP<\/p><p>Independent Repairers get authenticated by GIGYA CDC<\/p><p>On successful authentication, Ping Federate issues OIDC Access Token and redirects the user to the protected resource.<\/p><p>Akamai intercepts all request from browser to the origin – GDRP Application Load Balancer and also acts as reverse proxy for content &amp; documents published in Content Management System (AEMaaCS). Explained in detail in section 7.4.1<\/p><p>One of the Portal Function (backend microservice) – Security Component “Login Filter” – intercepts every request coming to load balancer.<\/p><p>Login Filter validates the Access Token with the Ping Federate OIDC “well known” endpoints and identifies the logged-in User ID.<\/p><p>Portal Security Component – Authorization Service – fetches authorization information from existing UAM system (summarized in section 1.2) and assess the roles &amp; permission to determine the information to be presented to the UI.<\/p><p>If the user has appropriate permission, associated Dealer Information is fetched from “periodically” loaded data in Platform’s native Relational Database. GDRP platform leverages many DB:<\/p><p>Relational DB – to store dealer data from regional dealer platform (CDDB for xF-NA and Webdac-Arcad for xP &amp; xF-EE). With <strong>Single Network Referential<\/strong><strong> <\/strong>becoming a reality, this local datastore will be phased out from the platform in future. Platform will integrate/migrate/adopt to Dealer Data Services coming out of Single Network Referential platform – Informatica.<\/p><p>NoSQL DB – to store the AEM’s content path &amp; its metadata for a given context.<\/p><p>Graph DB – to store Comments authored by various Portal Users on the article published by Business users in AEM.<\/p><p>Redis Cache – to store User session data minimizing the hits to SORs improving the performance of Portal Features.<\/p><p>One of the important features of platform is the ability to author and publish content for target audience. Platform has chosen Adobe Experience Manager as a Cloud Service (AEMaaCS) deployment model to harness the headless integration of AEM’s rich Web Content Management and Digital Asset Management capabilities.<\/p>", "text": "Before integrating any existing legacy web application or any go-to-market product-based web application or a new custom-built Greenfield web application with “The Dealer Experience” portal, it is important to understand a High-Level architecture component of the GDRP platform. The platform will evolve and mature with the ever-growing needs of the Integrating application by designing and developing reusable common component library.\n\nFigure 3- Platform Architecture Components\nGDRP platform has adopted a composite architecture for its portal feature leveraging Angular for frontend, AWS for Infrastructure & containerized backend microservices (BFF- Backend for Frontend) along with PaaS Persistent layers and SaaS Content Management Solution (CMS) from Adobe Experience Manager: \nA browser as a UI (User Interface) client act as the front-end interface through which users interact with web-based portal features. It initiates OpenID Connect flow to verify a user’s identity with the Stellantis’ OIDC server a.k.a. Global Ping Fed Server.\nDepending upon the type of User ID (described in section 1.3), Ping Federate redirects the client to regional authentication platform.\nDealers & Authorized Repairers of xP & xF-EE portals get authenticated by Active Directory (AD)\nInternal (HQ or Corporate) users of xP & xF-EE portals get authenticated either by Reunis or AD.\nUsers of xF-NA portal gets authenticated by NA Corporate LDAP\nIndependent Repairers get authenticated by GIGYA CDC\nOn successful authentication, Ping Federate issues OIDC Access Token and redirects the user to the protected resource.\nAkamai intercepts all request from browser to the origin – GDRP Application Load Balancer and also acts as reverse proxy for content & documents published in Content Management System (AEMaaCS). Explained in detail in section 7.4.1\nOne of the Portal Function (backend microservice) – Security Component “Login Filter” – intercepts every request coming to load balancer.\nLogin Filter validates the Access Token with the Ping Federate OIDC “well known” endpoints and identifies the logged-in User ID.\nPortal Security Component – Authorization Service – fetches authorization information from existing UAM system (summarized in section 1.2) and assess the roles & permission to determine the information to be presented to the UI.\nIf the user has appropriate permission, associated Dealer Information is fetched from “periodically” loaded data in Platform’s native Relational Database. GDRP platform leverages many DB:\nRelational DB – to store dealer data from regional dealer platform (CDDB for xF-NA and Webdac-Arcad for xP & xF-EE). With Single Network Referential becoming a reality, this local datastore will be phased out from the platform in future. Platform will integrate/migrate/adopt to Dealer Data Services coming out of Single Network Referential platform – Informatica.\nNoSQL DB – to store the AEM’s content path & its metadata for a given context.\nGraph DB – to store Comments authored by various Portal Users on the article published by Business users in AEM.\nRedis Cache – to store User session data minimizing the hits to SORs improving the performance of Portal Features.\nOne of the important features of platform is the ability to author and publish content for target audience. Platform has chosen Adobe Experience Manager as a Cloud Service (AEMaaCS) deployment model to harness the headless integration of AEM’s rich Web Content Management and Digital Asset Management capabilities."}, {"id": "d2-s7", "doc": 2, "title": "AEM as a Headless CMS solution", "html": "<p>Before we understand headless, let’s take a quick preview at traditional headful architecture. AEM as headful CMS architecture means that it handles both content management (backend) and content delivery (frontend). The CMS not only stores and manages content but also renders HTML through templating frameworks like <strong>HTL (HTML Template Language)<\/strong> or JSP. <\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 4-Headful CMS – a concept<\/p><p>In a nutshell, headless delivery takes away the page rendering responsibility from the CMS. The CMS expose data (content – text, path/reference to assets location – images, pdf etc..) as an API so that other application like Website (browser), Mobile, IoT, Kiosks etc. can consume it and render it. This is useful for omnichannel delivery, decoupled architecture, scalability, future proofing among others.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 5-Headless CMS – a concept<\/p><p>Please note that above representation depicts Client-API-CaaS (Content as a Service) in simplest representation, GDRP platform uses AWS hosted Java based microservices to enrich the content from AEM with the contextual information (geography, country, language etc.) of the user mashing up with dealer specific data for dealer users or regional data for corporate/HQ users from various legacy System of Records, ERP system, Flat files etc.<\/p><p>As describe earlier, in figure 3 of section 2.2 – frontend application sends the user’s access token to AWS Microservices to determine the context of the user (geography, country, language) from authorization system like MyPeople or MyPersonnel. These contexts are sent as part of request from AWS to AEMaaCS to fetch the content for that context and then mash it up with any application (modernized or legacy) data before serving it to the front end.<\/p><p>To make this whole process of fetching the content for a context - scalable &amp; performance enough and to be in sync with Content Store, GDRP adopted inspiration from the architecture explained in below article:<\/p><p>https://gspann.medium.com/how-to-use-aem-as-a-headless-cms-to-support-content-as-a-service-308ab035490a<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 6-Contextualized Content as a Service<\/p><p>While headless brings flexibility however it does bring one-time development overhead to map the frontend components with AEM components. The below diagram summarizes such mapping of components:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 7-High-level overview of mapping an AEM Component to Angular Component<\/p><p>Reference Article: https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/experience-manager-learn/getting-started-with-aem-headless/spa-editor/angular/map-components<\/p><p>Please note that GDRP’s frontend technology is <strong>Angular<\/strong> however frontend of Business Web Application can be any popular UI framework like React, Vue, NextJS etc. of course Angular included.<\/p>", "text": "Before we understand headless, let’s take a quick preview at traditional headful architecture. AEM as headful CMS architecture means that it handles both content management (backend) and content delivery (frontend). The CMS not only stores and manages content but also renders HTML through templating frameworks like HTL (HTML Template Language) or JSP. \n\nFigure 4-Headful CMS – a concept\nIn a nutshell, headless delivery takes away the page rendering responsibility from the CMS. The CMS expose data (content – text, path/reference to assets location – images, pdf etc..) as an API so that other application like Website (browser), Mobile, IoT, Kiosks etc. can consume it and render it. This is useful for omnichannel delivery, decoupled architecture, scalability, future proofing among others.\n\nFigure 5-Headless CMS – a concept\nPlease note that above representation depicts Client-API-CaaS (Content as a Service) in simplest representation, GDRP platform uses AWS hosted Java based microservices to enrich the content from AEM with the contextual information (geography, country, language etc.) of the user mashing up with dealer specific data for dealer users or regional data for corporate/HQ users from various legacy System of Records, ERP system, Flat files etc.\nAs describe earlier, in figure 3 of section 2.2 – frontend application sends the user’s access token to AWS Microservices to determine the context of the user (geography, country, language) from authorization system like MyPeople or MyPersonnel. These contexts are sent as part of request from AWS to AEMaaCS to fetch the content for that context and then mash it up with any application (modernized or legacy) data before serving it to the front end.\nTo make this whole process of fetching the content for a context - scalable & performance enough and to be in sync with Content Store, GDRP adopted inspiration from the architecture explained in below article:\nhttps://gspann.medium.com/how-to-use-aem-as-a-headless-cms-to-support-content-as-a-service-308ab035490a\n\nFigure 6-Contextualized Content as a Service\nWhile headless brings flexibility however it does bring one-time development overhead to map the frontend components with AEM components. The below diagram summarizes such mapping of components:\n\nFigure 7-High-level overview of mapping an AEM Component to Angular Component\nReference Article: https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/experience-manager-learn/getting-started-with-aem-headless/spa-editor/angular/map-components\nPlease note that GDRP’s frontend technology is Angular however frontend of Business Web Application can be any popular UI framework like React, Vue, NextJS etc. of course Angular included."}, {"id": "d2-s8", "doc": 2, "title": "Information Architecture of Portal", "html": "<p>Once a user has been authenticated and authorized, Platform first generates the Landing or Home page for the user as per entitlements. This page is assembled by the frontend client application based on the User’s context and the content from backend CMS component – AEMaaCS.<\/p><p>A typical landing page (LP) has following layout:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 8-Information Architecture of Landing Page<\/p><p>GDRP platform has defined Landing Page for each Business area. Currently, there are Landing Page templates defined for Sales, Aftersales or Service, HQ or Corporate persona categories.<\/p><p>All landing pages &amp; portal functionality pages has its layout defined in AEM and mapped to Frontend component (refer figure-7 in section 2.3).<\/p><p>Every component/element on Landing Page delivers portal capabilities (described in section 2.1). In summary, Header &amp; Footer are omnipresence component available for end users to interact at any point of time to access common functionality like Home, Search, Notification, My Account &amp; User Preferences, Logout and common articles like T&amp;C, Policy, Support &amp; Contact Us. Banner delivers hero image, primarily delivering marketing or impactful articles/materials for immediate attention from end users. Widgets are reusable user interface (UI) components that provides a specific piece of functionality or interactive element on a web page. Display of these Widgets on Landing Page can be enabled/disabled by end users using Widget Customization Wizard in User Preference function. <\/p><p>Following screen shot shows a Landing Page with header &amp; footer components functionality:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 9-Landing Page-Header Component<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 10-Landing Page-Footer Component<\/p>", "text": "Once a user has been authenticated and authorized, Platform first generates the Landing or Home page for the user as per entitlements. This page is assembled by the frontend client application based on the User’s context and the content from backend CMS component – AEMaaCS.\nA typical landing page (LP) has following layout:\n\nFigure 8-Information Architecture of Landing Page\nGDRP platform has defined Landing Page for each Business area. Currently, there are Landing Page templates defined for Sales, Aftersales or Service, HQ or Corporate persona categories.\nAll landing pages & portal functionality pages has its layout defined in AEM and mapped to Frontend component (refer figure-7 in section 2.3).\nEvery component/element on Landing Page delivers portal capabilities (described in section 2.1). In summary, Header & Footer are omnipresence component available for end users to interact at any point of time to access common functionality like Home, Search, Notification, My Account & User Preferences, Logout and common articles like T&C, Policy, Support & Contact Us. Banner delivers hero image, primarily delivering marketing or impactful articles/materials for immediate attention from end users. Widgets are reusable user interface (UI) components that provides a specific piece of functionality or interactive element on a web page. Display of these Widgets on Landing Page can be enabled/disabled by end users using Widget Customization Wizard in User Preference function. \nFollowing screen shot shows a Landing Page with header & footer components functionality:\n\nFigure 9-Landing Page-Header Component\n\nFigure 10-Landing Page-Footer Component"}, {"id": "d2-s9", "doc": 2, "title": "Application Integration Pattern", "html": "<p>Information or business processes/functions from application (new or legacy) can be integrated into GDRP platform in multiple ways based upon the experience the Business want to deliver to the portal’s end users. Does the Business want to share the information on Portal Landing Page or as a Business Application to be accessible from GDRP menu?<\/p>", "text": "Information or business processes/functions from application (new or legacy) can be integrated into GDRP platform in multiple ways based upon the experience the Business want to deliver to the portal’s end users. Does the Business want to share the information on Portal Landing Page or as a Business Application to be accessible from GDRP menu?"}, {"id": "d2-s10", "doc": 2, "title": "Integration with Portal Landing Page", "html": "<p>Widgets are purpose-built reusable component which are usually modular and can function independently &amp; may involve some form of user interaction (e.g. clicking, typing). Widgets can be purely content/information from CMS, or it can be hybrid i.e. Content (like Labels/Text, Image) from CMS combined with data from 3rd party system (non-GDRP hosted functional data). For e.g. a VIN lookup widget to be delivered in experience layer as below:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 11-Widget Examples<\/p><p>In the above example, <em><strong>Local Offer<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>s<\/strong><\/em> could be a pure content only widget with multiple cards being authored in AEM reflected by pagination in the widget. Clicking on <em><strong>Find Out More<\/strong><\/em> CTA (call to action) may open up an information <em><strong>Articl<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>e<\/strong><\/em> again to be authored in AEM. <\/p><p>If there is a need of such pure content-only information to be displayed on Landing Page in an “existing” Widget Template Library, there is no need for development. It should be authored using reusable infrastructure of GDRP i.e. AEMaaCS. Please note that an <em><strong>existing<\/strong><\/em> widget means that the Experience Component (Angular in GDRP) and the “mapped” AEM component were developed previously as a one-time development by the GDRP platform team – only to be re-used by Landing Page Layout Administrator.<\/p><p><em><strong>Car Selector<\/strong><\/em> is an example of Hybrid Widget, which has label/text such as <em><strong>car selector, Enter the VIN for Vehicle Information<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>,<\/strong><\/em> the text inside the button <em><strong>Search<\/strong><\/em> &amp; the <em><strong>vehicle ico<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>n<\/strong><\/em> image coming from AEM. After a successful search, the result could be designed to appear as shown below. Here, the text/label <em><strong>Make, Model, Year<\/strong><\/em> is delivered as content from AEM whereas the data (<em><strong>Peugeot, <\/strong><\/em><em><strong>308 SW Allure, 2025<\/strong><\/em>) is coming from a “non-GDRP hosted” VIN Lookup Application.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 12-Sample Application Widget – VIN Lookup Function<\/p><p>To generalize, the content and data is fetched from CMS and Business Application respectively while the experience i.e. the look &amp; feel of presenting the information in the UI is all taken care of by frontend application (Angular is adopted as UI framework for GDRP Portal capabilities’ experience layer).<\/p><p>To deliver above Widget experience, there could be 2 integration options provided by 3rd party Business Application.<\/p><p>Business Application data is exposed as API and GDRP Landing Page has the responsibility of generating the experience.<\/p><p>OR<\/p><p>Business Application data is delivered along with its native experience fragment i.e. HTML code is being received by GDRP frontend UI directly with no integration with GDRP’s BFF layer. <\/p><p>Let’s understand these 2 approaches in following sections:<\/p>", "text": "Widgets are purpose-built reusable component which are usually modular and can function independently & may involve some form of user interaction (e.g. clicking, typing). Widgets can be purely content/information from CMS, or it can be hybrid i.e. Content (like Labels/Text, Image) from CMS combined with data from 3rd party system (non-GDRP hosted functional data). For e.g. a VIN lookup widget to be delivered in experience layer as below:\n\nFigure 11-Widget Examples\nIn the above example, Local Offers could be a pure content only widget with multiple cards being authored in AEM reflected by pagination in the widget. Clicking on Find Out More CTA (call to action) may open up an information Article again to be authored in AEM. \nIf there is a need of such pure content-only information to be displayed on Landing Page in an “existing” Widget Template Library, there is no need for development. It should be authored using reusable infrastructure of GDRP i.e. AEMaaCS. Please note that an existing widget means that the Experience Component (Angular in GDRP) and the “mapped” AEM component were developed previously as a one-time development by the GDRP platform team – only to be re-used by Landing Page Layout Administrator.\nCar Selector is an example of Hybrid Widget, which has label/text such as car selector, Enter the VIN for Vehicle Information, the text inside the button Search & the vehicle icon image coming from AEM. After a successful search, the result could be designed to appear as shown below. Here, the text/label Make, Model, Year is delivered as content from AEM whereas the data (Peugeot, 308 SW Allure, 2025) is coming from a “non-GDRP hosted” VIN Lookup Application.\n\nFigure 12-Sample Application Widget – VIN Lookup Function\nTo generalize, the content and data is fetched from CMS and Business Application respectively while the experience i.e. the look & feel of presenting the information in the UI is all taken care of by frontend application (Angular is adopted as UI framework for GDRP Portal capabilities’ experience layer).\nTo deliver above Widget experience, there could be 2 integration options provided by 3rd party Business Application.\nBusiness Application data is exposed as API and GDRP Landing Page has the responsibility of generating the experience.\nOR\nBusiness Application data is delivered along with its native experience fragment i.e. HTML code is being received by GDRP frontend UI directly with no integration with GDRP’s BFF layer. \nLet’s understand these 2 approaches in following sections:"}, {"id": "d2-s11", "doc": 2, "title": "API based Integration", "html": "<p>Below phases are strongly suggested to be adopted for this type of integration with Landing Page.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 13-Application Widget Development Lifecycle<\/p><p><em><strong>Define Phase<\/strong><\/em> primarily driven by Business Group (LP) team and its back-office author team<\/p><p>They shall define the purpose and business objective of the widget<\/p><p>They shall work with back-office author team to define the target audience and the content aligning to the taxonomy available in AEM CMS<\/p><p><em><strong>Design Phase<\/strong><\/em> driven by inputs from Define phase with participation from Business Group (LP) team, its back-office Author team, GDRP development team and if 3rd party APIs involved then 3rd party API development team<\/p><p>Design the layout of the widget aligning with UX (stylesheet &amp; theme) of the LP<\/p><p>Design which data element displayed on widget are static coming out of AEM taxonomy and which data element are dynamic coming out of Business/Application APIs <\/p><p>If API doesn’t exist, identify the data source for development of such an API<\/p><p>If API exists, then analyze the data element to align with data needs of the widget as per the design<\/p><p><em><strong>Develop/Configure <\/strong><\/em><em><strong>P<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>hase<\/strong><\/em> involve construction of the widget by configuration &amp; coding as applicable<\/p><p>For a new type of widget, an entry in Widget Master (Library) shall be made to create a template for widget “type” generating the Widget ID<\/p><p>Angular Components shall be developed by GDRP UI Development Team &amp; Mapped AEM Component shall be developed by GDRP AEM Development Team to implement the design of the layout defined in Design phase<\/p><p>Either GDRP API or 3rd party API development team shall develop the API based upon the requirements of data element defined in Design phase<\/p><p>UI team shall map the frontend data handle with AEM Content &amp; API data element to bind the display to backend.<\/p><p><em><strong>Deploy/Author <\/strong><\/em><em><strong>P<\/strong><\/em><em><strong>hase<\/strong><\/em> involves development &amp; content authoring team to roll out the changes to the environment<\/p><p>For a given Widget ID, back-office authors the content in defined taxonomy<\/p><p>All 3 development tracks – UI, API &amp; AEM component are pushed via CICD pipeline to their respective target deployment platform<\/p><p>Author publishes the Widget in AEM to the target audience using tags &amp; taxonomy structure<\/p><p>Portal Landing Page layout has been explained in Section 3 and the integration of “experience” (UI frontend) with “Contextualized Content” from AEMaaCS in section 2.3.<\/p><p>The same architecture principle can be extended to bring in Application data (for e.g. VIN information) into Landing Page Widget Component.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 14-Contextualized Content with Application Data<\/p><p>At high-level following steps can be determined from above flow diagram:<\/p><p>Angular client application sends the VIN number to GDRP platform’s Microservice layer<\/p><p>Platforms security component validates the authenticity of request and also determines the context of the user (for e.g. language for label/text)<\/p><p>Platforms Microservice Layer would then execute the process to construct “enriched” JSON response<\/p><p>Extracting the VIN number from client request and after validating all integration security of Business API, it sends the VIN to remotely hosted VIN Lookup API &amp; receives the JSON response<\/p><p>Receives the content as JSON from headless AEMaaCS<\/p><p>Angular client receives the “enriched” JSON content from GDRP platforms Microservice Layer (BFF) and renders the experience on client-side browser agent.<\/p>", "text": "Below phases are strongly suggested to be adopted for this type of integration with Landing Page.\n\nFigure 13-Application Widget Development Lifecycle\nDefine Phase primarily driven by Business Group (LP) team and its back-office author team\nThey shall define the purpose and business objective of the widget\nThey shall work with back-office author team to define the target audience and the content aligning to the taxonomy available in AEM CMS\nDesign Phase driven by inputs from Define phase with participation from Business Group (LP) team, its back-office Author team, GDRP development team and if 3rd party APIs involved then 3rd party API development team\nDesign the layout of the widget aligning with UX (stylesheet & theme) of the LP\nDesign which data element displayed on widget are static coming out of AEM taxonomy and which data element are dynamic coming out of Business/Application APIs \nIf API doesn’t exist, identify the data source for development of such an API\nIf API exists, then analyze the data element to align with data needs of the widget as per the design\nDevelop/Configure Phase involve construction of the widget by configuration & coding as applicable\nFor a new type of widget, an entry in Widget Master (Library) shall be made to create a template for widget “type” generating the Widget ID\nAngular Components shall be developed by GDRP UI Development Team & Mapped AEM Component shall be developed by GDRP AEM Development Team to implement the design of the layout defined in Design phase\nEither GDRP API or 3rd party API development team shall develop the API based upon the requirements of data element defined in Design phase\nUI team shall map the frontend data handle with AEM Content & API data element to bind the display to backend.\nDeploy/Author Phase involves development & content authoring team to roll out the changes to the environment\nFor a given Widget ID, back-office authors the content in defined taxonomy\nAll 3 development tracks – UI, API & AEM component are pushed via CICD pipeline to their respective target deployment platform\nAuthor publishes the Widget in AEM to the target audience using tags & taxonomy structure\nPortal Landing Page layout has been explained in Section 3 and the integration of “experience” (UI frontend) with “Contextualized Content” from AEMaaCS in section 2.3.\nThe same architecture principle can be extended to bring in Application data (for e.g. VIN information) into Landing Page Widget Component.\n\nFigure 14-Contextualized Content with Application Data\nAt high-level following steps can be determined from above flow diagram:\nAngular client application sends the VIN number to GDRP platform’s Microservice layer\nPlatforms security component validates the authenticity of request and also determines the context of the user (for e.g. language for label/text)\nPlatforms Microservice Layer would then execute the process to construct “enriched” JSON response\nExtracting the VIN number from client request and after validating all integration security of Business API, it sends the VIN to remotely hosted VIN Lookup API & receives the JSON response\nReceives the content as JSON from headless AEMaaCS\nAngular client receives the “enriched” JSON content from GDRP platforms Microservice Layer (BFF) and renders the experience on client-side browser agent."}, {"id": "d2-s12", "doc": 2, "title": "Micro Frontend-based Integration", "html": "<p><strong>Micro-Frontend concept:<\/strong><strong> <\/strong>A &quot;micro frontend&quot; is a software architectural style where a web application&#x27;s front-end is broken down into smaller, independently deployable modules, allowing different teams to work on specific features within the application, develop them separately, and integrate them into a cohesive user interface at runtime. It is akin to micro services architecture in the server-side world.<\/p><p>The whole concept of Micro Frontend is well explained in following article:<\/p><p>https://medium.com/@kitson.mac/ui-micro-services-40798d2e3ef4<\/p><p>Unlike API based integration, typically in Micro Frontend style of integration with Business Application – the text/label, user interaction touchpoints like response data sorting, filter, search, buttons, CTA all gets encapsulated in Micro Frontend component and the UI Container Application i.e. in our case GDRP’s UI Angular Client Application loads the Micro Frontend component as a neatly encapsulated JavaScript library.<\/p><p>The whole concept of packaging &amp; delivering Micro Frontend to UI Container Application is explained in following article:<\/p><p>https://medium.com/@kitson.mac/ui-microservices-reversing-the-anti-pattern-375bc22287b0<\/p><p>At a high-level this type of integration can be contextualized to our example Widget as below:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 15-Micro Frontend based integration<\/p><p>Unlike API based integration with BFF layer, here the experience from GDRP platform and the remotely delivered experience from 3rd party application is mashed up at the UI Container Application running on the end users client-side agent/browser.<\/p><p>On load of GDRP’s Landing Page, Web Embeddable (JavaScript libraries) hosted on remote 3rd party are loaded as well<\/p><p>Applying contextuality to data is achieved by Single Sign On (SSO) script to be run as one-time global configuration (more on this later with a PoC example)<\/p><p>Data is from fetched from remote 3rd party application using Web Embeddable encapsulated calls hiding the complexity from UI Container Application<\/p><p>At the end, it is important to understand that 3rd Party Application should be flexible enough to export its functionality as Web Embeddable to enable this style of integration.<\/p><p>This integration pattern has been proven out as Proof of Concept by integrating ServiceNow Platform’s Web Embeddable component into GDRP’s Landing Page.<\/p><p>Stellantis has adopted ServiceNow as Incident Management tool for Dealer’s Vehicle Diagnostics Incident Management function. Stellantis has branded this Incident/Ticket Management platform as <strong>DigitalMe<\/strong> within the organization. ServiceNow’s Xanadou release allows extraction of case-list, case-view, case-create functionality as Web Embeddable.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 16-ServiceNow Case-List Micro Frontend<\/p><p>Below screen shot shows what all code was ingested into GDRP’s Landing Page UI:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 17-Global Configuration for SSO and load ServiceNow libraries<\/p><p>Few important things to note:<\/p><p>At line# 41 – ServiceNow JS libraries are imported by UI Container App<\/p><p>At line# 46 – UI Container App passes the OIDC access token (cached previously at local storage for session management during login process)<\/p><p>At line# 47 – relevant functional components from ServiceNow libraries are pre-loaded on client agent<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 18-ServiceNow Case-List Typescript Client Component<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 19-ServiceNow Case-List Presentation Component<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 20-GDRP Landing Page Client side include<\/p>", "text": "Micro-Frontend concept: A \"micro frontend\" is a software architectural style where a web application's front-end is broken down into smaller, independently deployable modules, allowing different teams to work on specific features within the application, develop them separately, and integrate them into a cohesive user interface at runtime. It is akin to micro services architecture in the server-side world.\nThe whole concept of Micro Frontend is well explained in following article:\nhttps://medium.com/@kitson.mac/ui-micro-services-40798d2e3ef4\nUnlike API based integration, typically in Micro Frontend style of integration with Business Application – the text/label, user interaction touchpoints like response data sorting, filter, search, buttons, CTA all gets encapsulated in Micro Frontend component and the UI Container Application i.e. in our case GDRP’s UI Angular Client Application loads the Micro Frontend component as a neatly encapsulated JavaScript library.\nThe whole concept of packaging & delivering Micro Frontend to UI Container Application is explained in following article:\nhttps://medium.com/@kitson.mac/ui-microservices-reversing-the-anti-pattern-375bc22287b0\nAt a high-level this type of integration can be contextualized to our example Widget as below:\n\nFigure 15-Micro Frontend based integration\nUnlike API based integration with BFF layer, here the experience from GDRP platform and the remotely delivered experience from 3rd party application is mashed up at the UI Container Application running on the end users client-side agent/browser.\nOn load of GDRP’s Landing Page, Web Embeddable (JavaScript libraries) hosted on remote 3rd party are loaded as well\nApplying contextuality to data is achieved by Single Sign On (SSO) script to be run as one-time global configuration (more on this later with a PoC example)\nData is from fetched from remote 3rd party application using Web Embeddable encapsulated calls hiding the complexity from UI Container Application\nAt the end, it is important to understand that 3rd Party Application should be flexible enough to export its functionality as Web Embeddable to enable this style of integration.\nThis integration pattern has been proven out as Proof of Concept by integrating ServiceNow Platform’s Web Embeddable component into GDRP’s Landing Page.\nStellantis has adopted ServiceNow as Incident Management tool for Dealer’s Vehicle Diagnostics Incident Management function. Stellantis has branded this Incident/Ticket Management platform as DigitalMe within the organization. ServiceNow’s Xanadou release allows extraction of case-list, case-view, case-create functionality as Web Embeddable.\n\nFigure 16-ServiceNow Case-List Micro Frontend\nBelow screen shot shows what all code was ingested into GDRP’s Landing Page UI:\n\nFigure 17-Global Configuration for SSO and load ServiceNow libraries\nFew important things to note:\nAt line# 41 – ServiceNow JS libraries are imported by UI Container App\nAt line# 46 – UI Container App passes the OIDC access token (cached previously at local storage for session management during login process)\nAt line# 47 – relevant functional components from ServiceNow libraries are pre-loaded on client agent\n\nFigure 18-ServiceNow Case-List Typescript Client Component\n\nFigure 19-ServiceNow Case-List Presentation Component\n\nFigure 20-GDRP Landing Page Client side include"}, {"id": "d2-s13", "doc": 2, "title": "Integration with Portal Menu", "html": "<p>This integration pattern is applicable to scenarios where Business Application Function (web pages) are being served as a standalone application from their own hosting environment. Such application may be an existing web application with modernized or legacy UI tech stack with its own stylesheets/themes or it may be a new Greenfield web application using GDRP’s design system (stylesheets &amp; web assets). Either of these applications can be configured from Portal menu and would become accessible to logged-in users based upon the authorization (security tags for AEM) fetched from either MyPersonnel or MyPeople based upon user’s entitlements.<\/p><p>Portal menu layout is self-explained in the screen shot below:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 21-GDRP Portal Menu layout (example)<\/p><p>Let’s better understand this integration pattern by taking an example of existing application and how to deliver a seamless experience to the end user by creating a façade that would make the end user feel that the application is being delivered from a common platform (instead of as 3rd party link out).<\/p><p>An example web application – Service Library – is shown below as a standalone web application delivering its own user experience and URL domain: https://library.fcaservices.com/web/secure/dashboard/user<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 22-Standalone application with its native experience &amp; domain address<\/p><p>This view obviously lacks the GDRP portal’s UI experience as it does not have Platform’s UI standards (Stylesheets &amp; themes) and also the URL in web browser would be different from the GDRP portal web address domain, intentionally because it is not served by the GDRP platform infrastructure.<\/p><p>Instead, the goal of integration approach described in this section, is to blend GDRP Platform’s omnipresence component – Header &amp; Footer – with adjustment being done to the native features of the integrating application:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 23-Unified Experience for 3rd Party Application – Target state<\/p><p>To deliver this experience, there are few design considerations that need to be accounted:<\/p>", "text": "This integration pattern is applicable to scenarios where Business Application Function (web pages) are being served as a standalone application from their own hosting environment. Such application may be an existing web application with modernized or legacy UI tech stack with its own stylesheets/themes or it may be a new Greenfield web application using GDRP’s design system (stylesheets & web assets). Either of these applications can be configured from Portal menu and would become accessible to logged-in users based upon the authorization (security tags for AEM) fetched from either MyPersonnel or MyPeople based upon user’s entitlements.\nPortal menu layout is self-explained in the screen shot below:\n\nFigure 21-GDRP Portal Menu layout (example)\nLet’s better understand this integration pattern by taking an example of existing application and how to deliver a seamless experience to the end user by creating a façade that would make the end user feel that the application is being delivered from a common platform (instead of as 3rd party link out).\nAn example web application – Service Library – is shown below as a standalone web application delivering its own user experience and URL domain: https://library.fcaservices.com/web/secure/dashboard/user\n\nFigure 22-Standalone application with its native experience & domain address\nThis view obviously lacks the GDRP portal’s UI experience as it does not have Platform’s UI standards (Stylesheets & themes) and also the URL in web browser would be different from the GDRP portal web address domain, intentionally because it is not served by the GDRP platform infrastructure.\nInstead, the goal of integration approach described in this section, is to blend GDRP Platform’s omnipresence component – Header & Footer – with adjustment being done to the native features of the integrating application:\n\nFigure 23-Unified Experience for 3rd Party Application – Target state\nTo deliver this experience, there are few design considerations that need to be accounted:"}, {"id": "d2-s14", "doc": 2, "title": "Single Sign On", "html": "<p>GDRP platform functions are secured by Stellantis OIDC server a.k.a. Global Ping Federate using Authorization Code Grant flow. This type of OIDC flow is very well explained in following article: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/oauth-20-authorization-code-grant-flow-naveen-rai-nxsbc<\/p><p>It is strongly suggested that the Integrating 3rd party application leverage the Ping Federate (SAML or OIDC) for user session information. This would ensure that when the end user navigates to the 3rd party application, browser would be able to SSO successfully.<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 24-Browser based SSO<\/p><p>In above example domain1 is GDRP platform domain viz., <strong>thedealerexperience.stellantis.com<\/strong> which is protected by Stellantis OIDC Auth Server (Global Ping Fed – domain3) at <strong>idfed.mpsa.com<\/strong> and 3rd party application (Service Library domain2 - <strong>library.stellantistools.com<\/strong>) is also federated to same Auth Server.<\/p>", "text": "GDRP platform functions are secured by Stellantis OIDC server a.k.a. Global Ping Federate using Authorization Code Grant flow. This type of OIDC flow is very well explained in following article: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/oauth-20-authorization-code-grant-flow-naveen-rai-nxsbc\nIt is strongly suggested that the Integrating 3rd party application leverage the Ping Federate (SAML or OIDC) for user session information. This would ensure that when the end user navigates to the 3rd party application, browser would be able to SSO successfully.\n\nFigure 24-Browser based SSO\nIn above example domain1 is GDRP platform domain viz., thedealerexperience.stellantis.com which is protected by Stellantis OIDC Auth Server (Global Ping Fed – domain3) at idfed.mpsa.com and 3rd party application (Service Library domain2 - library.stellantistools.com) is also federated to same Auth Server."}, {"id": "d2-s15", "doc": 2, "title": "Split Proxy", "html": "<p>Another aspect that needs to be addressed is the web address domain in the browser visible to the end user. Among many techniques is to make use of “Reverse Proxy” strategy from popular Content Delivery Network solution like Akamai, Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront etc. GDRP has adopted Stellantis existing enterprise CDN solution – Akamai. Role of CDN in GDRP platform has been explained later in section 7.4<\/p><p>With Split Proxy configured, the domain of 3rd party application will be masked behind GDRP platform domain as shown in screen shot below:<\/p><p><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\"><\/p><p>Figure 25-Unified Experience with GDRP web domain<\/p>", "text": "Another aspect that needs to be addressed is the web address domain in the browser visible to the end user. Among many techniques is to make use of “Reverse Proxy” strategy from popular Content Delivery Network solution like Akamai, Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront etc. GDRP has adopted Stellantis existing enterprise CDN solution – Akamai. Role of CDN in GDRP platform has been explained later in section 7.4\nWith Split Proxy configured, the domain of 3rd party application will be masked behind GDRP platform domain as shown in screen shot below:\n\nFigure 25-Unified Experience with GDRP web domain"}, {"id": "d2-s16", "doc": 2, "title": "Application Changes", "html": "<p>There could be many adjustments required for 3rd party application to create a seamless experience. Few of them are listed below:<\/p><p><strong>Relative URL<\/strong>: All references to web assets &amp; resources must be relative path. This would ensure that all the traffic to 3rd party application server is channelized through Split Proxy setup. If any of the CTA or HTTP request from 3rd party UI is initiated to absolute path, it may cause the browser to expose non-GDRP domain address.<\/p><p><strong>Native Functions<\/strong>: As shown in Figure 23, there could be many 3rd party application native features that need to be adjusted so as not to confuse the end user with overlapping functionality. A simplest example could be the “Welcome &lt;username&gt;” message native to the 3rd party application being duplicate to similar information in My Profile feature in GDRP header.<\/p><p><strong>Stylesheet &amp; Theme<\/strong>: This could be a very big change for any existing 3rd party application, which was primarily developed with no prior knowledge/references of GDRP platform UI standards. Fonts, Buttons, icons could have completely different themes as compared to pages delivered by Portal Function such as Landing Page, My Account, User Preferences etc.<\/p><p><strong>Header/Footer<\/strong>: Refer to section 7.2<\/p>", "text": "There could be many adjustments required for 3rd party application to create a seamless experience. Few of them are listed below:\nRelative URL: All references to web assets & resources must be relative path. This would ensure that all the traffic to 3rd party application server is channelized through Split Proxy setup. If any of the CTA or HTTP request from 3rd party UI is initiated to absolute path, it may cause the browser to expose non-GDRP domain address.\nNative Functions: As shown in Figure 23, there could be many 3rd party application native features that need to be adjusted so as not to confuse the end user with overlapping functionality. A simplest example could be the “Welcome <username>” message native to the 3rd party application being duplicate to similar information in My Profile feature in GDRP header.\nStylesheet & Theme: This could be a very big change for any existing 3rd party application, which was primarily developed with no prior knowledge/references of GDRP platform UI standards. Fonts, Buttons, icons could have completely different themes as compared to pages delivered by Portal Function such as Landing Page, My Account, User Preferences etc.\nHeader/Footer: Refer to section 7.2"}, {"id": "d2-s17", "doc": 2, "title": "Experience Layer", "html": "<p>Defining Experience Layer UI standards involves establishing consistent design principles, interaction patterns, and component behaviours to ensure a cohesive user experience. These standards guide development across teams, enhance usability, and promote brand consistency. They also support scalability, accessibility, and maintainability in evolving digital products and cross-platform user interfaces.<\/p>", "text": "Defining Experience Layer UI standards involves establishing consistent design principles, interaction patterns, and component behaviours to ensure a cohesive user experience. These standards guide development across teams, enhance usability, and promote brand consistency.
