first name<\/p><p>Article title<\/p><p>Article list<\/p><p>Portal link<\/p><p>Localized subject<\/p><p>Localized Thymeleaf template<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>buildEmail()<\/p>", "text": "Users without an email address are skipped.\nif (userObj.getEmail() == null) {\ncontinue;\n}\nFor every eligible user, the system creates an EmailMessage containing:\nRecipient email\nUsername and first name\nArticle title\nArticle list\nPortal link\nLocalized subject\nLocalized Thymeleaf template\nFunction:\nbuildEmail()"}, {"id": "d3-s22", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 19: Select the localized subject and template", "html": "<p>The user’s market determines the email subject and Thymeleaf template.<\/p><p>Examples include:<\/p><p>IT: Italian subject and template<\/p><p>ES: Spanish subject and template<\/p><p>FR: French subject and template<\/p><p>DE: German subject and template<\/p><p>PT or PR: Portuguese subject and template<\/p><p>NL: Dutch subject and template<\/p><p>DK: Danish subject and template<\/p><p>If the user market is not mapped, the implementation uses:<\/p><p>Subject: Newsletter Update<\/p><p>Template: emails/welcome-email<\/p><p>Functions:<\/p><p>extractEmailSubject()<\/p><p>extractEmailtemplate()<\/p>", "text": "The user’s market determines the email subject and Thymeleaf template.\nExamples include:\nIT: Italian subject and template\nES: Spanish subject and template\nFR: French subject and template\nDE: German subject and template\nPT or PR: Portuguese subject and template\nNL: Dutch subject and template\nDK: Danish subject and template\nIf the user market is not mapped, the implementation uses:\nSubject: Newsletter Update\nTemplate: emails/welcome-email\nFunctions:\nextractEmailSubject()\nextractEmailtemplate()"}, {"id": "d3-s23", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 20: Send email messages to the Email SQS queue", "html": "<p>The EmailMessage object is serialized into JSON.<\/p><p>String jsonString =    mapper.writeValueAsString(msg);<\/p><p>The system creates SQS batch entries containing:<\/p><p>Unique batch entry ID<\/p><p>Serialized EmailMessage payload<\/p><p>Message group ID<\/p><p>Message deduplication ID<\/p><p>The implementation sends messages in batches of five.<\/p><p>if (batchEntries.size() == 5) {<\/p><p>sendToSqs(batchEntries);<\/p><p>}<\/p><p>The producer sends to the queue URL configured by:<\/p><p>lpmi.sqs.queue.url<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>sendToSqs()<\/p>", "text": "The EmailMessage object is serialized into JSON.\nString jsonString =    mapper.writeValueAsString(msg);\nThe system creates SQS batch entries containing:\nUnique batch entry ID\nSerialized EmailMessage payload\nMessage group ID\nMessage deduplication ID\nThe implementation sends messages in batches of five.\nif (batchEntries.size() == 5) {\nsendToSqs(batchEntries);\n}\nThe producer sends to the queue URL configured by:\nlpmi.sqs.queue.url\nFunction:\nsendToSqs()"}, {"id": "d3-s24", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 21: Consume the Email SQS message", "html": "<p>EmailConsumer listens to the Email SQS queue configured by:<\/p><p>sqs.queue.email<\/p><p>Listener method:<\/p><p>@SqsListener(&quot;${sqs.queue.email}&quot;)<\/p><p>public void receiveDeleteMessage(...)<\/p><p>The consumer reads the JSON payload and converts it back into an EmailMessage.<\/p><p>EmailMessage msg =    mapper.readValue(payload, EmailMessage.class);<\/p><p>Functions:<\/p><p>receiveDeleteMessage()<\/p><p>processMessage()<\/p>", "text": "EmailConsumer listens to the Email SQS queue configured by:\nsqs.queue.email\nListener method:\n@SqsListener(\"${sqs.queue.email}\")\npublic void receiveDeleteMessage(...)\nThe consumer reads the JSON payload and converts it back into an EmailMessage.\nEmailMessage msg =    mapper.readValue(payload, EmailMessage.class);\nFunctions:\nreceiveDeleteMessage()\nprocessMessage()"}, {"id": "d3-s25", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 22: Validate the email message", "html": "<p>The consumer validates these required fields:<\/p><p>Recipient email<\/p><p>Username<\/p><p>News title<\/p><p>If the subject is missing, it creates a default subject:<\/p><p>Newsletter Update – {news title}<\/p><p>If the template is missing, it uses:<\/p><p>emails/welcome-email<\/p><p>The portal link is selected in this order:<\/p><p>1. EmailMessage portal link<\/p><p>2. Link from the first news item<\/p><p>3. Configured fallback should be used<\/p>", "text": "The consumer validates these required fields:\nRecipient email\nUsername\nNews title\nIf the subject is missing, it creates a default subject:\nNewsletter Update – {news title}\nIf the template is missing, it uses:\nemails/welcome-email\nThe portal link is selected in this order:\n1. EmailMessage portal link\n2. Link from the first news item\n3. Configured fallback should be used"}, {"id": "d3-s26", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 23: Prepare the Thymeleaf template variables", "html": "<p>The consumer prepares the variables required by the email template:<\/p><p>fullName<\/p><p>subject<\/p><p>newsList<\/p><p>portalLink<\/p><p>These variables are passed to MailService:<\/p><p>mailService.sendTemplatedEmail(    msg.getTo(),    subject,    template,    variables);<\/p>", "text": "The consumer prepares the variables required by the email template:\nfullName\nsubject\nnewsList\nportalLink\nThese variables are passed to MailService:\nmailService.sendTemplatedEmail(    msg.getTo(),    subject,    template,    variables);"}, {"id": "d3-s27", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 24: Apply email rate limiting", "html": "<p>Before sending an email, MailServiceImpl calls:<\/p><p>rateLimiter.acquire();<\/p><p>The rate limiter controls the email-sending rate and helps prevent the application from exceeding the configured SES sending capacity.<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>sendTemplatedEmail()<\/p>", "text": "Before sending an email, MailServiceImpl calls:\nrateLimiter.acquire();\nThe rate limiter controls the email-sending rate and helps prevent the application from exceeding the configured SES sending capacity.\nFunction:\nsendTemplatedEmail()"}, {"id": "d3-s28", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 25: Render the HTML email", "html": "<p>The selected Thymeleaf template is processed with the supplied variables.<\/p><p>templateEngine.process(finalTemplate, context);<\/p><p>The result is the final HTML email body.<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>renderTemplate()<\/p>", "text": "The selected Thymeleaf template is processed with the supplied variables.\ntemplateEngine.process(finalTemplate, context);\nThe result is the final HTML email body.\nFunction:\nrenderTemplate()"}, {"id": "d3-s29", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 26: Build the Amazon SES request", "html": "<p>The implementation creates an Amazon SES SendEmailRequest containing:<\/p><p>Configured sender address<\/p><p>Recipient email address<\/p><p>Localized subject<\/p><p>Rendered HTML email body<\/p><p>UTF-8 character set<\/p><p>The sender address comes from:<\/p><p>app.email.from<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>buildRequest()<\/p>", "text": "The implementation creates an Amazon SES SendEmailRequest containing:\nConfigured sender address\nRecipient email address\nLocalized subject\nRendered HTML email body\nUTF-8 character set\nThe sender address comes from:\napp.email.from\nFunction:\nbuildRequest()"}, {"id": "d3-s30", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 27: Send the email through Amazon SES", "html": "<p>The final email is sent using:<\/p><p>sesClient.sendEmail(request);<\/p><p>If successful, Amazon SES returns a message ID, which is written to the application log.<\/p><p>Function:<\/p><p>sendWithRetry()<\/p>", "text": "The final email is sent using:\nsesClient.sendEmail(request);\nIf successful, Amazon SES returns a message ID, which is written to the application log.\nFunction:\nsendWithRetry()"}, {"id": "d3-s31", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 28: Retry transient SES failures", "html": "<p>The implementation retries the SES operation when the error code is:<\/p><p>Throttling<\/p><p>TooManyRequestsException<\/p><p>The maximum number of attempts is:<\/p><p>MAX_RETRIES = 3;<\/p><p>Exponential backoff is applied between attempts.<\/p><p>Non-retryable errors are thrown immediately.<\/p><p>Functions:<\/p><p>isRetryable()<\/p><p>backoff()<\/p>", "text": "The implementation retries the SES operation when the error code is:\nThrottling\nTooManyRequestsException\nThe maximum number of attempts is:\nMAX_RETRIES = 3;\nExponential backoff is applied between attempts.\nNon-retryable errors are thrown immediately.\nFunctions:\nisRetryable()\nbackoff()"}, {"id": "d3-s32", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 29: Acknowledge the Email SQS message", "html": "<p>After the email is successfully sent through SES, the consumer acknowledges the Email SQS message.<\/p><p>acknowledgement.acknowledge();<\/p><p>If email processing throws an exception, the acknowledgement is not executed.<\/p><p>The exception is logged for retry handling according to the SQS listener and queue configuration.<\/p>", "text": "After the email is successfully sent through SES, the consumer acknowledges the Email SQS message.\nacknowledgement.acknowledge();\nIf email processing throws an exception, the acknowledgement is not executed.\nThe exception is logged for retry handling according to the SQS listener and queue configuration."}, {"id": "d3-s33", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 30: Update the article-event status", "html": "<p>After enqueueSendEmail() completes, the scheduler marks the article event as PROCESSED. This status confirms that scheduler processing completed; it does not by itself confirm that every recipient email was successfully delivered by Amazon SES.<\/p><p>PROCESSED<\/p><p>If general processing fails, it updates the event as:<\/p><p>FAILED<\/p><p>and stores the error message in remarks.<\/p><p>For the following business conditions, the current implementation marks the event as PROCESSED and records the reason:<\/p><p>AEM response is null<\/p><p>No news found in AEM<\/p><p>No users found<\/p><p>Processing guarantees and assumptions: Message delivery is asynchronous and may be retried by SQS. Duplicate prevention for article events is based on the article ID. A PROCESSED article-event status indicates completion of scheduler processing, not confirmed delivery to every recipient. Queue visibility timeouts, redrive policies, dead-letter queues, and retention settings are operational dependencies and should be verified in the deployment configuration.<\/p>", "text": "After enqueueSendEmail() completes, the scheduler marks the article event as PROCESSED. This status confirms that scheduler processing completed; it does not by itself confirm that every recipient email was successfully delivered by Amazon SES.\nPROCESSED\nIf general processing fails, it updates the event as:\nFAILED\nand stores the error message in remarks.\nFor the following business conditions, the current implementation marks the event as PROCESSED and records the reason:\nAEM response is null\nNo news found in AEM\nNo users found\nProcessing guarantees and assumptions: Message delivery is asynchronous and may be retried by SQS. Duplicate prevention for article events is based on the article ID. A PROCESSED article-event status indicates completion of scheduler processing, not confirmed delivery to every recipient. Queue visibility timeouts, redrive policies, dead-letter queues, and retention settings are operational dependencies and should be verified in the deployment configuration."}, {"id": "d3-s34", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: Article-Event Status", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>Article received<\/strong><\/td><td>A new article event is stored with status NEW.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Scheduler processing<\/strong><\/td><td>The scheduler selects and processes eligible NEW or FAILED events.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Successful completion<\/strong><\/td><td>The event is marked PROCESSED after scheduler processing completes.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Processing failure<\/strong><\/td><td>The event is marked FAILED and may be selected by a later scheduler run.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Retry outcome<\/strong><\/td><td>A retried event is updated to PROCESSED or remains FAILED.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 2. Article-Event Status Flow<\/p><p><strong>5. Important configuration properties<\/strong><\/p><p>The flow depends on the following application properties:<\/p><p># Global content-event SQS queue<\/p><p>sqs.queue.global.lpmi<\/p><p># Email SQS listener queue<\/p><p>sqs.queue.email<\/p><p># Email SQS producer queue URL<\/p><p>lpmi.sqs.queue.url<\/p><p># Scheduler enable or disable switch<\/p><p>email.app.scheduler.switch<\/p><p># LPMI portal base URL<\/p><p>app.env.url<\/p><p># Email sender address<\/p><p>app.email.from<\/p><p>The following two properties must refer to the same email queue:<\/p><p>sqs.queue.email<\/p><p>lpmi.sqs.queue.url<\/p><p>Typically, one contains the queue name used by the listener annotation, while the other contains the queue URL used by the SQS client.<\/p><p>@SqsListener<\/p><p>SqsClient<\/p><p><strong>6. Important error-handling points<\/strong><\/p><p><strong>Global SQS producer<\/strong><\/p><p>The Global SQS producer catches SQS exceptions and returns a failure message. The /publish controller currently does not check the returned result.<\/p><p>sendGlobalMessage()<\/p><p>This means the API can return HTTP 200 even when sending to Global SQS fails.<\/p><p><strong>Global SQS consumer<\/strong><\/p><p>The receiver catches exceptions internally. If it does not rethrow the exception, the outer method may acknowledge the message even though content processing failed.<\/p><p>processContentItem()<\/p><p><strong>Email SQS producer<\/strong><\/p><p>The Email SQS producer logs batch failures but does not throw an exception back to the scheduler.<\/p><p>sendToSqs()<\/p><p>As a result, an article event can potentially be marked as PROCESSED even when some email messages were not successfully sent to SQS.<\/p><p><strong>Email SQS consumer validation<\/strong><\/p><p>For missing recipient, username, or news title, EmailConsumer returns without explicitly acknowledging the message.<\/p><p>If manual acknowledgement is configured, these permanently invalid messages may be received again after the SQS visibility timeout.<\/p><p><strong>Email delivery <\/strong><strong>retry<\/strong><\/p><p>MailServiceImpl retries only SES throttling-related errors. Other errors are treated as non-retryable and are thrown back to the Email SQS consumer.<\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nArticle received\nA new article event is stored with status NEW.\n2\nScheduler processing\nThe scheduler selects and processes eligible NEW or FAILED events.\n3\nSuccessful completion\nThe event is marked PROCESSED after scheduler processing completes.\n4\nProcessing failure\nThe event is marked FAILED and may be selected by a later scheduler run.\n5\nRetry outcome\nA retried event is updated to PROCESSED or remains FAILED.\nTable 2. Article-Event Status Flow\n5. Important configuration properties\nThe flow depends on the following application properties:\n# Global content-event SQS queue\nsqs.queue.global.lpmi\n# Email SQS listener queue\nsqs.queue.email\n# Email SQS producer queue URL\nlpmi.sqs.queue.url\n# Scheduler enable or disable switch\nemail.app.scheduler.switch\n# LPMI portal base URL\napp.env.url\n# Email sender address\napp.email.from\nThe following two properties must refer to the same email queue:\nsqs.queue.email\nlpmi.sqs.queue.url\nTypically, one contains the queue name used by the listener annotation, while the other contains the queue URL used by the SQS client.\n@SqsListener\nSqsClient\n6. Important error-handling points\nGlobal SQS producer\nThe Global SQS producer catches SQS exceptions and returns a failure message. The /publish controller currently does not check the returned result.\nsendGlobalMessage()\nThis means the API can return HTTP 200 even when sending to Global SQS fails.\nGlobal SQS consumer\nThe receiver catches exceptions internally. If it does not rethrow the exception, the outer method may acknowledge the message even though content processing failed.\nprocessContentItem()\nEmail SQS producer\nThe Email SQS producer logs batch failures but does not throw an exception back to the scheduler.\nsendToSqs()\nAs a result, an article event can potentially be marked as PROCESSED even when some email messages were not successfully sent to SQS.\nEmail SQS consumer validation\nFor missing recipient, username, or news title, EmailConsumer returns without explicitly acknowledging the message.\nIf manual acknowledgement is configured, these permanently invalid messages may be received again after the SQS visibility timeout.\nEmail delivery retry\nMailServiceImpl retries only SES throttling-related errors. Other errors are treated as non-retryable and are thrown back to the Email SQS consumer."}, {"id": "d3-s35", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: End-to-End Article Notification", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>Receive and queue<\/strong><\/td><td>AEM calls POST /publish; the controller reads each item, adds sequenceId, and sends LPMI content to Global SQS.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Process content event<\/strong><\/td><td>The Global SQS consumer performs page or cache invalidation and checks duplicate article IDs.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Retrieve and store article<\/strong><\/td><td>The latest article data is retrieved from AEM with retry handling and stored as an ArticleEvent with status NEW.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Select recipients<\/strong><\/td><td>The hourly scheduler selects eligible events, extracts targeting metadata, resolves JR codes, and retrieves users.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Create and queue emails<\/strong><\/td><td>Localized EmailMessage payloads are created and sent to Email SQS in batches.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>6<\/td><td><strong>Render and send<\/strong><\/td><td>EmailConsumer validates each message, prepares Thymeleaf variables, renders HTML, and sends through Amazon SES.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>7<\/td><td><strong>Acknowledge and update<\/strong><\/td><td>The Email SQS message is acknowledged after SES accepts the email; the scheduler separately updates the ArticleEvent status.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 3. End-to-End Article Notification Flow<\/p><p><strong>Writing improvements<\/strong><\/p><p>The flow is organized into clear processing stages with the actual class names, functions, statuses, queue properties, retry behavior, and acknowledgement points. It also separates the normal business flow from current error-handling risks, making the section suitable for both technical documentation and architecture review.<\/p><p><strong>Purpose of /<\/strong><strong>publishNotifications<\/strong><\/p><p>The purpose of /publishNotifications is to create, update, or delete the <strong>notification records displayed in the LPMI portal<\/strong>.<\/p><p><strong>What it does<\/strong><\/p><p>Receives one or more content events.<\/p><p>Sends each content item to the Publish Notification SQS queue.<\/p><p>The SQS listener consumes each content event.<\/p><p>For a delete event, it removes the notification using the content ID.<\/p><p>For a create or update event, it deletes the existing notification first.<\/p><p>Retrieves the latest notification content from AEM.<\/p><p>Parses notification fields such as title, description, image, dates, link, role tags, geographical tags, and brand tags.<\/p><p>Converts the information into NotificationEntity records.<\/p><p>Batch-saves the notification records into the configured LPMI notification table.<\/p><p>Acknowledges the SQS message after successful processing.<\/p><p><strong>Simple purpose statement for your document<\/strong><\/p><p>The /publishNotifications API maintains the notification records displayed in the LPMI Portal. It processes content events asynchronously, retrieves the latest notification data from AEM, and creates, updates, or deletes records in the configured LPMI notification table.<\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nReceive and queue\nAEM calls POST /publish; the controller reads each item, adds sequenceId, and sends LPMI content to Global SQS.\n2\nProcess content event\nThe Global SQS consumer performs page or cache invalidation and checks duplicate article IDs.\n3\nRetrieve and store article\nThe latest article data is retrieved from AEM with retry handling and stored as an ArticleEvent with status NEW.\n4\nSelect recipients\nThe hourly scheduler selects eligible events, extracts targeting metadata, resolves JR codes, and retrieves users.\n5\nCreate and queue emails\nLocalized EmailMessage payloads are created and sent to Email SQS in batches.\n6\nRender and send\nEmailConsumer validates each message, prepares Thymeleaf variables, renders HTML, and sends through Amazon SES.\n7\nAcknowledge and update\nThe Email SQS message is acknowledged after SES accepts the email; the scheduler separately updates the ArticleEvent status.\nTable 3. End-to-End Article Notification Flow\nWriting improvements\nThe flow is organized into clear processing stages with the actual class names, functions, statuses, queue properties, retry behavior, and acknowledgement points. It also separates the normal business flow from current error-handling risks, making the section suitable for both technical documentation and architecture review.\nPurpose of /publishNotifications\nThe purpose of /publishNotifications is to create, update, or delete the notification records displayed in the LPMI portal.\nWhat it does\nReceives one or more content events.\nSends each content item to the Publish Notification SQS queue.\nThe SQS listener consumes each content event.\nFor a delete event, it removes the notification using the content ID.\nFor a create or update event, it deletes the existing notification first.\nRetrieves the latest notification content from AEM.\nParses notification fields such as title, description, image, dates, link, role tags, geographical tags, and brand tags.\nConverts the information into NotificationEntity records.\nBatch-saves the notification records into the configured LPMI notification table.\nAcknowledges the SQS message after successful processing.\nSimple purpose statement for your document\nThe /publishNotifications API maintains the notification records displayed in the LPMI Portal. It processes content events asynchronously, retrieves the latest notification data from AEM, and creates, updates, or deletes records in the configured LPMI notification table."}, {"id": "d3-s36", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: Portal Notification Maintenance", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>POST /<\/strong><strong>publishNotifications<\/strong><\/td><td>Receives one or more create, update, or delete content events.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Publish Notification SQS<\/strong><\/td><td>Queues each content item for asynchronous processing.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Delete decision<\/strong><\/td><td>Delete events remove the matching notification record and finish.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Create or update<\/strong><\/td><td>Removes the existing record, retrieves the latest data from AEM, and parses the notification details.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Persist notifications<\/strong><\/td><td>Converts LPMI notification data into entities and batch-saves them in the configured table.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 4. Portal Notification Maintenance Flow<\/p><p><strong>Important Processing Steps<\/strong><\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nPOST /publishNotifications\nReceives one or more create, update, or delete content events.\n2\nPublish Notification SQS\nQueues each content item for asynchronous processing.\n3\nDelete decision\nDelete events remove the matching notification record and finish.\n4\nCreate or update\nRemoves the existing record, retrieves the latest data from AEM, and parses the notification details.\n5\nPersist notifications\nConverts LPMI notification data into entities and batch-saves them in the configured table.\nTable 4. Portal Notification Maintenance Flow\nImportant Processing Steps"}, {"id": "d3-s37", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 1: Receive the notification request", "html": "<p>The client sends a request containing one or more content items to:<\/p><p>POST /publishNotifications<\/p><p>The controller passes the complete request to:<\/p><p>sqsMessageSender.processPushNotifications(requestBody);<\/p>", "text": "The client sends a request containing one or more content items to:\nPOST /publishNotifications\nThe controller passes the complete request to:\nsqsMessageSender.processPushNotifications(requestBody);"}, {"id": "d3-s38", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 2: Send each content item to SQS", "html": "<p>The request is converted into a ContentPath object.<\/p><p>Each Content item is:<\/p><p>Serialized into JSON.<\/p><p>Sent as an individual message to the queue configured by:<\/p><p>sqs.queue.publishNotification<\/p><p>This allows the notification records to be processed asynchronously.<\/p>", "text": "The request is converted into a ContentPath object.\nEach Content item is:\nSerialized into JSON.\nSent as an individual message to the queue configured by:\nsqs.queue.publishNotification\nThis allows the notification records to be processed asynchronously."}, {"id": "d3-s39", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 3: Consume the SQS message", "html": "<p>The method below listens to the Publish Notification SQS queue:<\/p><p>publishNotificationListen()<\/p><p>It:<\/p><p>Reads the SQS payload.<\/p><p>Converts the JSON payload into a Content object.<\/p><p>Calls:<\/p><p>notificationService.saveNotificationsFromAEM(content);<\/p>", "text": "The method below listens to the Publish Notification SQS queue:\npublishNotificationListen()\nIt:\nReads the SQS payload.\nConverts the JSON payload into a Content object.\nCalls:\nnotificationService.saveNotificationsFromAEM(content);"}, {"id": "d3-s40", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 4: Process delete events", "html": "<p>When:<\/p><p>eventType = delete<\/p><p>the service deletes the existing notification using the content ID:<\/p><p>notificationDao.deleteNotificationById(    lpmiNotTable,    content.getId());<\/p><p>No AEM call or new database insertion is performed for delete events.<\/p>", "text": "When:\neventType = delete\nthe service deletes the existing notification using the content ID:\nnotificationDao.deleteNotificationById(    lpmiNotTable,    content.getId());\nNo AEM call or new database insertion is performed for delete events."}, {"id": "d3-s41", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 5: Process create or update events", "html": "<p>For non-delete events, the service:<\/p><p>Deletes the existing notification with the same content ID.<\/p><p>Retrieves the latest content information from AEM.<\/p><p>Parses the AEM response.<\/p><p>Creates new notification records.<\/p><p>This follows a delete-and-reinsert approach.<\/p>", "text": "For non-delete events, the service:\nDeletes the existing notification with the same content ID.\nRetrieves the latest content information from AEM.\nParses the AEM response.\nCreates new notification records.\nThis follows a delete-and-reinsert approach."}, {"id": "d3-s42", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 6: Retrieve the latest content from AEM", "html": "<p>The latest notification data is retrieved using:<\/p><p>aemSpringRestClient.pageData(content, role, false);<\/p><p>The expected AEM response contains:<\/p><p>pageComponents<\/p><p>    └── data<\/p>", "text": "The latest notification data is retrieved using:\naemSpringRestClient.pageData(content, role, false);\nThe expected AEM response contains:\npageComponents\n    └── data"}, {"id": "d3-s43", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 7: Parse the notification information", "html": "<p>The service processes the AEM pageComponents and extracts important fields such as:<\/p><p>Notification ID<\/p><p>Article ID<\/p><p>Title<\/p><p>Description<\/p><p>Image<\/p><p>Link path<\/p><p>Start date<\/p><p>Created date<\/p><p>Brand tags<\/p><p>Role tags<\/p><p>Geographical tags<\/p><p>Deep-link indicator<\/p><p>Content type<\/p><p>The extracted values are stored in NotificationDTO objects.<\/p>", "text": "The service processes the AEM pageComponents and extracts important fields such as:\nNotification ID\nArticle ID\nTitle\nDescription\nImage\nLink path\nStart date\nCreated date\nBrand tags\nRole tags\nGeographical tags\nDeep-link indicator\nContent type\nThe extracted values are stored in NotificationDTO objects."}, {"id": "d3-s44", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 8: Save only LPMI notifications", "html": "<p>Notification records are saved only when:<\/p><p>contentType = lpmi<\/p><p>The service calls:<\/p><p>saveNotifications(notificationDTOs, lpmiNotTable);<\/p>", "text": "Notification records are saved only when:\ncontentType = lpmi\nThe service calls:\nsaveNotifications(notificationDTOs, lpmiNotTable);"}, {"id": "d3-s45", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 9: Convert DTOs into database entities", "html": "<p>Each NotificationDTO is converted into a NotificationEntity.<\/p><p>The entity includes:<\/p><p>Partition key<\/p><p>Sort key<\/p><p>Notification ID<\/p><p>Article ID<\/p><p>Title<\/p><p>Description<\/p><p>Dates<\/p><p>Tags<\/p><p>Link path<\/p><p>Image<\/p><p>Deep-link indicator<\/p>", "text": "Each NotificationDTO is converted into a NotificationEntity.\nThe entity includes:\nPartition key\nSort key\nNotification ID\nArticle ID\nTitle\nDescription\nDates\nTags\nLink path\nImage\nDeep-link indicator"}, {"id": "d3-s46", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 10: Save records in the notification table", "html": "<p>The notification entities are batch-saved using:<\/p><p>notificationDao.putBatchRecords(    notifications,    tableNotification);<\/p><p>The destination table is configured through:<\/p><p>lpmi.notification.table<\/p>", "text": "The notification entities are batch-saved using:\nnotificationDao.putBatchRecords(    notifications,    tableNotification);\nThe destination table is configured through:\nlpmi.notification.table"}, {"id": "d3-s47", "doc": 3, "title": "Step 11: Acknowledge the SQS message", "html": "<p>After notification processing completes successfully, the listener acknowledges the SQS message.<\/p><p>Acknowledgement.acknowledge(message);<\/p><p>If processing fails, the exception is logged and rethrown, and the normal acknowledgement step is not completed.<\/p>", "text": "After notification processing completes successfully, the listener acknowledges the SQS message.\nAcknowledgement.acknowledge(message);\nIf processing fails, the exception is logged and rethrown, and the normal acknowledgement step is not completed."}, {"id": "d3-s48", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: Event-Type Decision", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>Evaluate event type<\/strong><\/td><td>The service checks whether eventType is delete.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Delete path<\/strong><\/td><td>For a delete event, the matching notification record is removed and processing finishes.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Create or update path<\/strong><\/td><td>For a non-delete event, the existing record is removed and the latest data is retrieved from AEM.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Parse content<\/strong><\/td><td>The AEM response is parsed into notification information.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Persist LPMI records<\/strong><\/td><td>When contentType is lpmi, the notification records are saved.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 5. Event-Type Decision Flow<\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nEvaluate event type\nThe service checks whether eventType is delete.\n2\nDelete path\nFor a delete event, the matching notification record is removed and processing finishes.\n3\nCreate or update path\nFor a non-delete event, the existing record is removed and the latest data is retrieved from AEM.\n4\nParse content\nThe AEM response is parsed into notification information.\n5\nPersist LPMI records\nWhen contentType is lpmi, the notification records are saved.\nTable 5. Event-Type Decision Flow"}, {"id": "d3-s49", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: Portal Notification Processing", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>Receive request<\/strong><\/td><td>A client calls POST /publishNotifications with one or more content items.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Queue content items<\/strong><\/td><td>The request is converted into ContentPath data and each item is sent separately to Publish Notification SQS.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Consume message<\/strong><\/td><td>The listener converts each SQS message back into a Content object.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Apply event action<\/strong><\/td><td>Delete events remove the notification; non-delete events remove the existing record before refresh.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Retrieve and parse<\/strong><\/td><td>The latest content is retrieved from AEM and converted into NotificationDTO objects.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>6<\/td><td><strong>Persist records<\/strong><\/td><td>LPMI DTOs are converted into NotificationEntity records and batch-saved.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>7<\/td><td><strong>Acknowledge message<\/strong><\/td><td>The SQS message is acknowledged after successful processing.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 6. Portal Notification Processing Flow<\/p><p><strong>POST /<\/strong><strong>getNotificationsByUserName<\/strong><strong>: User Notification Retrieval<\/strong><\/p><p><strong>Purpose<\/strong><\/p><p>The /getNotificationsByUserName API retrieves notifications applicable to a specific portal user. Eligibility is determined from the user’s role, market, region, language, and content path; the response also indicates whether each notification has been read.<\/p><p><strong>Important Flow Steps<\/strong><\/p><p>The Portal UI calls:<\/p><p>POST /getNotificationsByUserName<\/p><p>The API extracts and validates the following user information:<\/p><p>User name<\/p><p>User type<\/p><p>Market<\/p><p>Region<\/p><p>Current role<\/p><p>Language<\/p><p>Common notification records are retrieved from the DynamoDB notification table using:<\/p><p>PK = NOTIFICATION#NOTIFICATION<\/p><p>SK starts with NOTIFICATION#<\/p><p>Common notifications are filtered using:<\/p><p>User role against notification role tags<\/p><p>User market against notification geographical tags<\/p><p>User region, market, and language against the notification link path<\/p><p>Global notification path<\/p><p>An empty role-tag list applies to all roles, and an empty geographical-tag list applies to all markets.<\/p><p>User-specific notification records are retrieved using:<\/p><p>PK = USER#{userName}<\/p><p>These records identify notifications already read by the user.<\/p><p>Comment notifications associated with the user are retrieved using:<\/p><p>PK = COMMENT#{userName}<\/p><p>Common notifications are marked as read when a corresponding user record exists with the same notification sort key.<\/p><p>Matching USER record found    → isRead = true<\/p><p>Matching USER record not found → isRead = false<\/p><p>Common notifications and user comment notifications are combined into one list.<\/p><p>Notifications with a null or future startDate are excluded.<\/p><p>The remaining notifications are sorted by startDate in descending order, with the newest notification first.<\/p><p>The result is limited to the latest 50 notifications.<\/p><p>The final notification list is returned to the Portal UI.<\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nReceive request\nA client calls POST /publishNotifications with one or more content items.\n2\nQueue content items\nThe request is converted into ContentPath data and each item is sent separately to Publish Notification SQS.\n3\nConsume message\nThe listener converts each SQS message back into a Content object.\n4\nApply event action\nDelete events remove the notification; non-delete events remove the existing record before refresh.\n5\nRetrieve and parse\nThe latest content is retrieved from AEM and converted into NotificationDTO objects.\n6\nPersist records\nLPMI DTOs are converted into NotificationEntity records and batch-saved.\n7\nAcknowledge message\nThe SQS message is acknowledged after successful processing.\nTable 6. Portal Notification Processing Flow\nPOST /getNotificationsByUserName: User Notification Retrieval\nPurpose\nThe /getNotificationsByUserName API retrieves notifications applicable to a specific portal user. Eligibility is determined from the user’s role, market, region, language, and content path; the response also indicates whether each notification has been read.\nImportant Flow Steps\nThe Portal UI calls:\nPOST /getNotificationsByUserName\nThe API extracts and validates the following user information:\nUser name\nUser type\nMarket\nRegion\nCurrent role\nLanguage\nCommon notification records are retrieved from the DynamoDB notification table using:\nPK = NOTIFICATION#NOTIFICATION\nSK starts with NOTIFICATION#\nCommon notifications are filtered using:\nUser role against notification role tags\nUser market against notification geographical tags\nUser region, market, and language against the notification link path\nGlobal notification path\nAn empty role-tag list applies to all roles, and an empty geographical-tag list applies to all markets.\nUser-specific notification records are retrieved using:\nPK = USER#{userName}\nThese records identify notifications already read by the user.\nComment notifications associated with the user are retrieved using:\nPK = COMMENT#{userName}\nCommon notifications are marked as read when a corresponding user record exists with the same notification sort key.\nMatching USER record found    → isRead = true\nMatching USER record not found → isRead = false\nCommon notifications and user comment notifications are combined into one list.\nNotifications with a null or future startDate are excluded.\nThe remaining notifications are sorted by startDate in descending order, with the newest notification first.\nThe result is limited to the latest 50 notifications.\nThe final notification list is returned to the Portal UI."}, {"id": "d3-s50", "doc": 3, "title": "Flow Summary: User Notification Retrieval", "html": "<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table><tr><td>Step<\/td><td>Stage<\/td><td>What happens<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>1<\/td><td><strong>Portal request<\/strong><\/td><td>The Portal UI calls POST /getNotificationsByUserName.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>2<\/td><td><strong>Validate user context<\/strong><\/td><td>Validates username, user type, market, region, role, and language.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>3<\/td><td><strong>Query DynamoDB<\/strong><\/td><td>Retrieves common notifications, user read-status records, and comment notifications.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>4<\/td><td><strong>Filter eligibility<\/strong><\/td><td>Filters common notifications by role, market, region, language, and content path.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>5<\/td><td><strong>Calculate read status<\/strong><\/td><td>Marks a common notification as read when the matching user record exists.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>6<\/td><td><strong>Combine and clean<\/strong><\/td><td>Combines lists and removes notifications with null or future start dates.<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>7<\/td><td><strong>Sort and limit<\/strong><\/td><td>Sorts newest first and returns the latest 50 notifications.<\/td><\/tr><\/table><\/div><p>Table 7. User Notification Retrieval Flow<\/p><p><strong>Notification Eligibility Rules<\/strong><\/p><p>A common notification is shown to the user when:<\/p><p>Role matches or notification has no role restriction<\/p><p>AND<\/p><p>Market matches or notification has no market restriction<\/p><p>AND<\/p><p>Notification belongs to the user&#x27;s market-specific path or global path<\/p><p>The market-specific path is constructed as:<\/p><p>/content/experience-fragments/lpmi/{region}/{market}/{language}/<\/p><p><strong>Error Handling<\/strong><\/p><p>If required fields are missing or processing fails, the API returns an error inside the response object with:<\/p><p>Error code: 400<\/p><p>HTTP status: 400<\/p><p>Error message: Applicable validation or processing error<\/p><p><strong>Short Summary<\/strong><\/p><p>The /getNotificationsByUserName API retrieves common and user-specific notifications from DynamoDB, filters them according to the user’s role, market, region, and language, determines their read status, removes future notifications, and returns the latest 50 notifications to the LPMI Portal.<\/p><p><strong>Writing improvements<\/strong><\/p><p>The flow retains only the main API, DynamoDB query, filtering, read-status, sorting, limiting, and response steps. Detailed implementation methods and supporting article or banner functions were excluded because they are not part of this API flow.<\/p>", "text": "Step\nStage\nWhat happens\n1\nPortal request\nThe Portal UI calls POST /getNotificationsByUserName.\n2\nValidate user context\nValidates username, user type, market, region, role, and language.\n3\nQuery DynamoDB\nRetrieves common notifications, user read-status records, and comment notifications.\n4\nFilter eligibility\nFilters common notifications by role, market, region, language, and content path.\n5\nCalculate read status\nMarks a common notification as read when the matching user record exists.\n6\nCombine and clean\nCombines lists and removes notifications with null or future start dates.\n7\nSort and limit\nSorts newest first and returns the latest 50 notifications.\nTable 7. User Notification Retrieval Flow\nNotification Eligibility Rules\nA common notification is shown to the user when:\nRole matches or notification has no role restriction\nAND\nMarket matches or notification has no market restriction\nAND\nNotification belongs to the user's market-specific path or global path\nThe market-specific path is constructed as:\n/content/experience-fragments/lpmi/{region}/{market}/{language}/\nError Handling\nIf required fields are missing or processing fails, the API returns an error inside the response object with:\nError code: 400\nHTTP status: 400\nError message: Applicable validation or processing error\nShort Summary\nThe /getNotificationsByUserName API retrieves common and user-specific notifications from DynamoDB, filters them according to the user’s role, market, region, and language, determines their read status, removes future notifications, and returns the latest 50 notifications to the LPMI Portal.\nWriting improvements\nThe flow retains only the main API, DynamoDB query, filtering, read-status, sorting, limiting, and response steps. Detailed implementation methods and supporting article or banner functions were excluded because they are not part of this API flow."}, {"id": "d4-s1", "doc": 4, "title": "Slide 1 · DealerX  Platform", "html": "<ul><li>DealerX<\/li><li> Platform<\/li><li>Overview<\/li><li> and SDK <\/li><li>Guidelines<\/li><li>Onboarding<\/li><li>3/12/2025<\/li><\/ul>", "text": "DealerX\n Platform\nOverview\n and SDK \nGuidelines\n \nOnboarding\n \n3/12/2025"}, {"id": "d4-s2", "doc": 4, "title": "Slide 2 · Agenda DealerX", "html": "<ul><li>Agenda<\/li><li>DealerX<\/li><li>: <\/li><li>Why<\/li><li>it<\/li><li>Matters<\/li><li>DealerX<\/li><li> – The <\/li><li>solution<\/li><li>Platform Architecture in a Nutshell<\/li><li>AEM as a Headless CMS solution<\/li><li>Landing Page Architecture<\/li><li>Application Integration Pattern<\/li><li>Application Development<\/li><li>SDK Adoption<\/li><li>Common Component Library<\/li><li>Useful Links<\/li><li>Q&amp;A<\/li><\/ul><img loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Source document figure\" src=\"data:image/png;base64,\">", "text": "Agenda\nDealerX\n: \nWhy\n \nit\n \nMatters\nDealerX\n – The \nsolution\nPlatform Architecture in a Nutshell\nAEM as a Headless CMS solution\nLanding Page Architecture\nApplication Integration Pattern\nApplication Development\nSDK Adoption\nCommon Component Library\nUseful Links\nQ&A"}, {"id": "d4-s3", "doc": 4, "title": "Slide 3 · DealerX : ", "html": "<ul><li>DealerX<\/li><li>: <\/li><li>Why<\/li><li>it<\/li><li>Matters<\/li><li>Under the <\/li><li>Dare <\/li><li>Forward<\/li><li> 2030<\/li><li> strategy, <\/li><li>Stellantis<\/li><li>aims<\/li><li> to <\/li><li>unify<\/li><li> the <\/li><li>digital<\/li><li>experience<\/li><li> for dealers and <\/li><li>repairers<\/li><li>through<\/li><li>: <\/li><li>DealerX<\/li><li>. <\/li><li>The solution is a platform to promote a new digital workplace to enhance synergies and efficiencies, at dealer and at business level; 4, "title": "Slide 6 · AEM as a Headless CMS solution In the ", "html": "<ul><li>AEM as a Headless CMS solution<\/li><li>In the <\/li><li>DealerX<\/li><li> platform, <\/li><li>AEM<\/li><li> is "text": "Thank \nyou\nQ&A\n3/12/2025"}, {"id": "d5-s1", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 1 · Development Standards Reference", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">Development Standards Reference\n\n\nVersion 3.0 – Cloud &amp; Software Engineering – Stellantis\n\nAuthor: Cloud &amp; Software Engineering – Stellantis\n\nAudience: Developers, Tech Leads, Architects, DevOps, Quality, External Partners\n\nLast Updated: November 27, 2025\n\n\n1. Introduction\nThis document outlines the Stellantis Cloud &amp; Software Engineering standards, intended to\nguide teams and suppliers in delivering software that is consistent, high-quality, and secure.\nThese standards are designed for all stakeholders in the software lifecycle, including\ndevelopers, architects, technical leads, DevOps engineers, and external partners. The\nstandards are living, actionable, and aligned with enterprise best practices, supporting both\ninternal and supplier-driven development processes.\n\n\n2. Objectives\n    •   Standardize development practices to promote consistency, efficiency, and\n        interoperability across all projects.\n    •  Promote high standards of quality, security, maintainability, and scalability for all\n        deliverables.\n    •   Accelerate onboarding and operational support through clear, actionable blueprints\n      and platform engineering.\n    •  Enable seamless integration and collaboration across the technology landscape.\n    •   Institute measurable governance, continuous improvement, and actionable\n       feedback mechanisms.\n\n\n3. Blueprints &amp; Developer Experience\nStellantis offers standardized blueprints, including one-click templates and reference\narchitectures, integrated within the platform engineering toolkit. These blueprints address\ncommon use cases such as microservices, event-driven APIs, and mobile apps, expediting\nonboarding for both internal teams and suppliers. Platform engineering practices ensure a\nconsistent developer experience, providing automated environment provisioning, security\ndefaults, and integrated documentation.\nCSWE Blueprint Github repository<\/div>", "text": "Development Standards Reference\n\n\nVersion 3.0 – Cloud & Software Engineering – Stellantis\n\nAuthor: Cloud & Software Engineering – Stellantis\n\nAudience: Developers, Tech Leads, Architects, DevOps, Quality, External Partners\n\nLast Updated: November 27, 2025\n\n\n1. Platform engineering practices ensure a\nconsistent developer experience, providing automated environment provisioning, security\ndefaults, and integrated documentation.\nCSWE Blueprint Github repository"}, {"id": "d5-s2", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 2 · 4. Recommended Languages & Frameworks", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">4. Recommended Languages &amp; Frameworks\nStellantis chooses languages and frameworks based on alignment with enterprise needs,\nperformance, extensibility, and prevailing industry trends. This selection is reviewed and\nupdated regularly to reflect technology advances and developer feedback. The following\nsections provide guidance for each major technology category, outlining the rationale and\ntypical applications for each.\n\n4.1 Backend\nBackend technologies are selected for robustness, scalability, and suitability for enterprise-\nscale applications. The chosen languages and frameworks address a variety of use cases,\nfrom high-performance microservices to data-intensive APIs:\n\n    •   Java (Spring Boot, Quarkus): Java is a foundational language for enterprise\n      development due to its maturity, extensive ecosystem, and long-term support.\n       Spring Boot simplifies microservices and REST API development with rapid setup,\n       strong security, and broad adoption. Quarkus is optimized for Kubernetes and\n       cloud-native deployments, offering fast startup and low memory usage for modern,\n       containerized environments.\n    •  Python (FastAPI, Flask): Python&#x27;s simplicity and versatility make it well-suited for\n       data-driven services, machine learning APIs, and lightweight backends. FastAPI is\n       recognized for high performance and intuitive design, while Flask is ideal for rapid\n       prototyping and smaller services.\n    •   TypeScript (NestJS, Fastify, Hapi.js): TypeScript is favored for backend development\n      due to its strong typing, scalability, and seamless integration with modern\n        JavaScript tooling. NestJS provides a robust, modular architecture ideal for building\n       enterprise-grade APIs and microservices. Fastify is recognized for its high\n       performance and low overhead, making it suitable for latency-sensitive and scalable\n        applications. Hapi.js offers rich configuration capabilities and plugin support,\n      making it a solid choice for building secure and extensible server solutions.\n    •  Rust (Actix, Rocket): Rust provides memory safety and exceptional performance,\n      making it suitable for systems programming and performance-critical services. Actix\n        offers high throughput for web servers, and Rocket enhances developer productivity\n       with a type-safe API.\n\n\n    Tier     Language  Framework               Typical Use Cases\n                          / Tech\n                                     Core enterprise microservices and high-\n                          Spring Boot, Backend    Java                      throughput transactional APIs and backends\n                        Quarkus\n                                           integrating with legacy platforms.\n                                  Data/ML model APIs, event-driven and\n                            FastAPI,       serverless workloads (integration, automation,\n Backend    Python                           Flask         glue code), as well as lightweight internal\n                                       backends.<\/div>", "text": "4. Architecture & Design", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">5. Architecture &amp; Design\nPreferred architectural styles include microservices, API-driven (REST, GraphQL), and\nevent-driven architectures. Blueprints guide the adoption of Clean Architecture, Domain-\nDriven Design (DDD), the 12-Factor App methodology, and SOLID principles. API design\nstandards require the use of OpenAPI v3 (Swagger) and API gateways such as Apigee or\nAWS API Gateway, with templates available for rapid integration.\n\nFor CI/CD and deployment, cloud-native approaches are prioritized to maximize scalability,\nmaintainability, and resilience. While containerization technologies such as Docker and\nKubernetes offer portability and isolation, their use should be reserved for specific\nscenarios where they provide clear benefits—such as supporting legacy workloads,\ncomplex multi-service orchestration, or custom runtime requirements. In most cases,\nleveraging managed cloud services and serverless platforms is preferred to reduce\noperational overhead and accelerate delivery. Containers should not be the default\ndeployment model but rather a targeted solution for well-justified use cases.\n\nThis section defines preferred architectural styles and guiding principles for modern\napplication development, providing explanations to inform technical architects and\ndevelopers.\n\n5.1 Microservices\nMicroservices architecture structures applications as small, independent services that\ninteract over well-defined APIs.\n\n    •  Each service is self-contained and focused on a specific business capability.\n    •   Services can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.\n    •  Technology stacks and data storage solutions may differ between services.\n    •  Communication typically uses lightweight protocols such as HTTP/REST or\n       messaging queues.\n\nBenefits: Improved scalability and resilience, faster development cycles, easier deployment,\nenhanced maintainability, and flexibility.\n\nChallenges: Increased complexity in orchestration and communication, potential data\nconsistency and transaction management issues, and the need for robust monitoring and\nautomation.\n\n5.2 REST (Representational State Transfer)\nREST is an architectural style for networked applications that relies on stateless, client-\nserver communication, typically over HTTP(S).\n\n    •   Stateless interactions: Each request includes all necessary information.\n    •  Resources are identified by URIs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods\n       (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).\n    •  Adheres to layered system and uniform interface constraints.<\/div>", "text": "5. Architecture & Design\nPreferred architectural styles include microservices, API-driven (REST, GraphQL), and\nevent-driven architectures. Blueprints guide the adoption of Clean Architecture, Domain-\nDriven Design (DDD), the 12-Factor App methodology, and SOLID principles. In most cases,\nleveraging managed cloud services and serverless platforms is preferred to reduce\noperational overhead and accelerate delivery. Containers should not be the default\ndeployment model but rather a targeted solution for well-justified use cases.\n\nThis section defines preferred architectural styles and guiding principles for queues.\n\nBenefits: Improved scalability and resilience, faster development cycles, easier deployment,\nenhanced maintainability, and flexibility.\n\nChallenges: Increased complexity in orchestration is widely adopted for web APIs, microservices communication, and mobile\napplications due to its simplicity and interoperability.\n\n5.3 GraphQL\nGraphQL is a query language for APIs that allows clients to request exactly the data they\nneed, minimizing over-fetching and under-fetching.\n\n    •   Clients specify the structure of the response.\n    •   Single endpoint for queries and mutations.\n    •   Strongly typed schema enables introspection and validation.\n\nComparison with REST: Unlike REST, which uses multiple endpoints for different resources,\nGraphQL aggregates data from various sources and returns it in a single response,\nimproving efficiency and flexibility for complex applications with strong data linkage (if\nimplemented correctly).\n\n5.4 Event-Driven Architecture\nEvent-driven architecture (EDA) is a paradigm where system components communicate by\ngenerating, detecting, and consuming events.\n\n    •  Event Producers: Generate events upon state changes.\n    •  Event Consumers: Listen for and respond to events.\n    •  Event Brokers: Route events between producers and consumers using\n       intermediaries such as message queues or event buses.\n\nBenefits: Loose coupling, improved scalability and responsiveness, support for\nasynchronous processing, and real-time updates.\n\n5.5 Clean Architecture\nClean Architecture structures code into layers to emphasize separation of concerns and\nindependence from frameworks, databases, and user interfaces.\n\n    •   Entities: Core business logic and data structures.\n    •  Use Cases: Application-specific business rules.\n    •   Interface Adapters: Convert data between external sources and internal\n       representations.\n    •  Frameworks &amp; Drivers: External tools, databases, and frameworks.\n\nThis organization promotes testability, maintainability, and adaptability to change.\n\n5.7 12-Factor App Methodology\nThe 12-Factor App methodology guides the development of modern, cloud-native\napplications that are scalable, maintainable, and portable. Its factors include:\n\n    1.  Codebase\n    2. Our primary cloud-native options are:\n\n    •  Aurora DB (AWS): The preferred managed relational database service on AWS,\n       compatible with both PostgreSQL and MySQL. Aurora offers high performance,\n         scalability, and automated management, making it suitable for modern cloud-native\n        applications.\n    •  Azure Database for PostgreSQL / Azure Database for MySQL: Azure’s managed\n        offerings for PostgreSQL and MySQL provide enterprise-grade security, high\n         availability, and scalability. These tools help ensure consistency and traceability of database\nmigrations across development, testing, and production environments.\n\nSecurity Best Practices: Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, and\nencrypt storage for sensitive data.\n\n Database                 Primary Use Case\n Aurora DB (AWS)           Cloud-native, scalable, managed SQL workloads on AWS\n Azure Database             Cloud-native, managed SQL workloads on Azure\n PostgreSQL                Legacy, high-complexity, or Oracle-competitive workloads\n\n\nNoSQL Databases\nNoSQL databases are ideal for semi-structured, hierarchical, or rapidly evolving schemas.\nOur recommended options include:\n\n    •  DynamoDB: Managed NoSQL database on AWS, offering high scalability and\n       performance for key-value and document workloads.\n    •  Cosmos DB: Azure’s globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database supporting\n       document, key-value, and graph data models.\n    •  MongoDB: Popular for handling flexible, semi-structured data.\n    •  DocumentDB: Managed document database compatible with MongoDB on AWS; use\n      Azure Cosmos DB for similar use cases on Azure.\n\nChoose the NoSQL solution based on scalability needs, cloud provider alignment, and data\nmodel requirements.\n\n Database                            Primary Use Case\n DynamoDB                                  Scalable key-value/document storage\n                                    (AWS)\n Cosmos DB                                  Scalable key-value/document storage\n                                           (Azure)\n DocumentDB                         Managed MongoDB-compatible (AWS)\n MongoDB                                 Semi-structured data (restricted or legacy)<\/div>", "text": "automate schema changes. services:\n\n    •  Amazon ElastiCache: Highly available, scalable Redis on AWS.\n    •  Azure Cache for Redis: Managed Redis service on Azure.\n\nBoth options provide advanced caching, session management, and pub/sub messaging to\nenhance application performance.\n\n Service                              Primary Use Case\n ElastiCache (Redis)                         Caching, session management (AWS)\n Azure Cache for Redis                       Caching, session management (Azure)\n\nObject/Binary Storage\nFor storing objects, large binary data, backups, and media, use:\n\n    •  Amazon S3: Industry-standard object storage on AWS, supporting versioning,\n        lifecycle policies, and encryption.\n    •  Azure Blob Storage: Highly scalable object storage on Azure for unstructured data.\n\n Service                              Primary Use Case\n Amazon S3                                Binary/object storage (AWS)\n Azure Blob "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">    •  For AWS Lambda, consider using the AWS Lambda Power Tuning tool, which can\n       help identify the optimal cost/performance ratio for your functions. This tool\n       provides valuable insights for designing efficient memory allocation strategies.\n\nTimeout Configuration\n    •   Define precise timeout periods for each function to prevent unwanted resource\n        utilization and costs.\n    •  Review and adapt timeouts as application logic evolves.\n\nError Handling and Retry Policies\n    •   Establish structured error handling with dedicated code paths for recoverable and\n         fatal errors.\n    •   Configure native retry mechanisms: AWS Lambda supports asynchronous retries;\n      Azure Functions allow custom retry strategies.\n    •  Monitor and log all exceptions for rapid troubleshooting.\n\nDead Letter Queues (DLQ) for Failed Invocations\n    •  Enable DLQs to route failed invocations safely for follow-up analysis and\n       remediation.\n    •   Integrate with SQS/SNS (AWS) or Service Bus/Storage Queues (Azure).\n    •   Regularly audit DLQ contents to identify recurring problems.\n\nConcurrency Limits and Throttling\n    •   Set reserved concurrency (AWS) or adjust scaling limits (Azure) to protect\n       resources and ensure fairness.\n    •  Monitor and respond to throttling events by tuning limits or scaling capacity.\n\nSecrets Management (Beyond Environment Variables)\n    •   Store sensitive credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault (or other\n      CSP native services like AWS System Manager etc..), not in environment variables.\n    •  Enforce granular access controls and automated secret rotation.\n    •  Audit all access to secrets and automate updates for reduced risk.\n\nOptimization (Provisioned Concurrency, Reserved Capacity, Cost or Performance)\n    •  Leverage provisioned concurrency (AWS Lambda) and pre-warmed instances\n       (Azure Premium) for stable, predictable workloads.\n    •   Routinely review usage analytics to eliminate underutilized resources and automate\n       scaling/cleanup.<\/div>", "text": "    •  For AWS Lambda, consider using the AWS Lambda Power Tuning tool, which can\n       help identify the optimal cost/performance ratio for your functions. This tool\n       provides valuable insights for designing efficient memory allocation strategies.\n\nTimeout Configuration\n    •   Define precise timeout periods for each function to prevent unwanted resource\n        utilization and costs.\n    •  Review and adapt timeouts as application logic evolves.\n\nError Handling and Retry Policies\n    •   Establish structured error handling with dedicated code paths for recoverable and\n         fatal errors.\n    •   Configure native retry mechanisms: AWS Lambda supports asynchronous retries;\n      Azure Functions allow custom retry strategies.\n    •  Monitor and log all exceptions for rapid troubleshooting.\n\nDead Letter Queues (DLQ) for Failed Invocations\n    •  Enable DLQs to route failed invocations safely for follow-up analysis and\n       remediation.\n    •   Integrate with SQS/SNS (AWS) or Service Bus/Storage Queues (Azure).\n    •   Regularly audit DLQ contents to identify recurring problems.\n\nConcurrency Limits and Throttling\n    •   Set reserved concurrency (AWS) or adjust scaling limits (Azure) to protect\n       resources and ensure fairness.\n    •  Monitor and respond to throttling events by tuning limits or scaling capacity.\n\nSecrets Management (Beyond Environment Variables)\n    •   Store sensitive credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault (or other\n      CSP native services like AWS System Manager etc..), not in environment variables.\n    •  Enforce granular access controls and automated secret rotation.\n    •  Audit all access to secrets and automate updates for reduced risk.\n\nOptimization (Provisioned Concurrency, Reserved Capacity, Cost or Performance)\n    •  Leverage provisioned concurrency (AWS Lambda) and pre-warmed instances\n       (Azure Premium) for stable, predictable workloads.\n    •   Routinely review usage analytics to eliminate underutilized resources and automate\n       scaling/cleanup."}, {"id": "d5-s12", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 12 · 7.3 Documentation and Architectural Guidance", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">7.3 Documentation and Architectural Guidance\nFor in-depth blueprints, architectural patterns, and compliance references, please consult\nthe Stellantis Global Landing Zone documentation on our SharePoint portal.\n\n\n8. Mobile Development\nMobile development embraces a variety of approaches, each with its own strengths and\nbest-fit scenarios. The three primary strategies are cross-platform development, native iOS\ndevelopment, and native Android development. Below, each choice is detailed to help clarify\ntheir unique advantages, technology stack, and ideal use cases.\n\n8.1 Cross-Platform Development\nCross-platform development leverages Flutter and the Dart programming language to build\nmobile applications that run efficiently on both iOS and Android from a single codebase.\nThis approach is particularly well-suited for B2E (Business-to-Employee) and B2B\n(Business-to-Business) mobile apps, where consistency and rapid feature deployment\nacross multiple platforms are key. Cross-platform frameworks accelerate onboarding and\nreduce maintenance costs, while blueprints help enforce security defaults such as OAuth2\nwith PKCE and local data encryption. Integration with services like Firebase and Sentry, as\nwell as code obfuscation, further enhance app robustness and monitoring.\n\n8.2 Native iOS Development\nNative iOS development utilizes Swift and SwiftUI to create applications that fully leverage\nthe capabilities of Apple devices. This approach is best for projects requiring a high-end\nuser experience and deep integration with the iOS ecosystem—such as advanced UI\ntransitions, native APIs (e.g., Apple Pay, ARKit), and device-specific features. Native\ndevelopment offers superior performance, security, and access to the latest iOS innovations.\nBlueprints streamline onboarding and enforce best practices for OAuth2 with PKCE, local\nencryption, and seamless integration with tools like Firebase and Sentry, while also\nproviding guidance for code obfuscation to safeguard intellectual property.\n\n8.3 Native Android Development\nNative Android development is built on Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, providing full access to\nthe Android platform&#x27;s capabilities. This method is ideal for delivering the complete\nAndroid experience, including custom UI components, direct integration with system-level\nfeatures (such as Google Play Services, notifications, and background tasks), and optimal\nperformance on a wide variety of devices. Security defaults are established through\nblueprints (OAuth2 with PKCE, local encryption), and integrations with Firebase, Sentry,\nand code obfuscation tools are readily available to enhance reliability and protect\ncodebases.\n\n Approach               Tech                   Use Case<\/div>", "text": "7.3 Documentation and Architectural Guidance\nFor in-depth blueprints, architectural patterns, and compliance references, please consult\nthe Stellantis Global Landing Zone documentation on our SharePoint portal.\n\n\n8. Testing &amp; Quality\nComprehensive software testing forms the backbone of reliable, secure applications that\ndeliver a consistent user experience. The testing process encompasses multiple levels, each\ntailored to validate different aspects of the software, using specialized tools and approaches.\nBy incorporating a unified testing platform—such as Appvance, OpenText, or Tricentis—\norganizations can streamline and centralize test management, automation, and reporting,\nwhich greatly facilitates coordination across teams and technologies.\n\nTesting Types and Their Application\nUnit Testing: Unit tests focus on validating individual components or functions in isolation,\nensuring each behaves as intended. These tests are typically executed early in the\ndevelopment process and are best suited for local development and continuous integration\n(CI) pipelines. Common tools for unit testing include JUnit for Java, PyTest for Python, and\nJest for JavaScript.\n\nIntegration Testing: Integration tests verify that different modules or services interact\ncorrectly. These tests are conducted after unit tests and before deploying to higher\nenvironments, confirming that APIs, databases, and external services function together as\nexpected. Tools such POSTMAN, REST-assured are frequently used for integration testing.\n\nEnd-to-End / UI Testing: End-to-end and user interface (UI) tests simulate complete user\nworkflows from start to finish, validating the system as a whole. These tests are ideal for\npre-release validation and should be executed in staging environments that closely mirror\nproduction. Cypress and Selenium are popular choices for this type of testing.\n\nSecurity Testing: Security testing aims to identify vulnerabilities and insecure coding\npractices. It should be performed continuously during development and prior to any\nrelease. Modern platforms enable the integration of security scans directly into CI/CD\npipelines for automated enforcement. Github Advanced Security will be our corporate tool.\n\nPerformance Testing: Performance tests evaluate the application&#x27;s responsiveness,\nstability, and scalability under load. These tests are best conducted in dedicated\nenvironments that replicate real-world traffic and usage conditions, particularly before\nmajor releases. JMeter and k6 are standard tools for performance testing.<\/div>", "text": " Cross-platform                Flutter (Dart)             B2E/B2B mobile apps,\n                                                       shared codebase, rapid\n                                                             delivery\n Native iOS                    Swift / SwiftUI              High-end UX, deep iOS\n                                                                integration, cutting-edge\n                                                     Apple features\n Native Android               Kotlin / Jetpack Compose     Full Android experience,\n                                                              platform-specific\n                                                                 capabilities\n\n\n\n9. These platforms centralize scheduling, execution, reporting, and\nanalytics, making it easier to enforce quality gates—such as minimum coverage, linting, and\nsupplier validation—and to ensure all code submissions are reviewed and meet required\nstandards. This centralized approach is particularly valuable for complex projects involving\nmultiple teams, diverse technologies, and rigorous compliance requirements.\n\nBy leveraging unified testing platforms, organizations can automate quality gates, enforce\nconsistent standards, and maintain visibility across the entire testing lifecycle, ensuring\nrobust and secure software delivery.\n\n10. Security &amp; Compliance\n\n10.1 Security and Compliance Overview\nSecurity and compliance are essential considerations throughout the entire software\ndevelopment lifecycle. With the integration of GitHub Advanced Security (GAS), code\nrepositories benefit from advanced protection mechanisms that help identify vulnerabilities\nand insecure coding practices. The GAS suite includes Code Scanning, Secret Scanning, and\nDependency Review, which are automated as part of the CI/CD pipeline. These scans serve\nas security gates, ensuring that any code merges or deployments are subject to rigorous\nchecks before being approved.\n\n10.2 Static Application Security Testing (SAST)\nStatic Application Security Testing is conducted using the code scanning capabilities\nprovided by GitHub Advanced Security. This approach replaces previous tools such as\nCheckmarx. GHAS integrates directly with GitHub repositories to scan source code for\nsecurity vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and policy violations. By identifying issues early\nin the development process, teams can remediate risks before they reach production.\n\n10.3 Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)\nDynamic Application Security Testing is performed using tools like OWASP ZAP. These tools\nsimulate real-world attacks against running applications to uncover runtime vulnerabilities.\nResults from DAST scans are incorporated into automated compliance gates, which can\nblock deployments if critical issues are detected, ensuring that only secure code moves\nforward.<\/div>", "text": " Type                                  Tools\n Unit Tests                                       JUnit, PyTest, Jest, SonarQube(for report)\n Tests Plan                        TBD with Testing Platform\n Integration                        TBD with Testing Platform\n End-to-End / UI                    TBD with Testing Platform\n Security                          TBD with Testing Platform\n Performance                       TBD with Testing Platform\n\nRole of Unified Testing Platforms\nUnified testing platforms like Appvance, OpenText, and Tricentis provide an integrated\nenvironment for managing all types of tests, including unit, integration, end-to-end,\nsecurity, and performance. These tools\nsimulate real-world attacks against running applications to uncover runtime vulnerabilities.\nResults from DAST scans are incorporated into automated compliance gates, which can\nblock deployments if critical issues are detected, ensuring that only secure code moves\nforward."}, {"id": "d5-s15", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 15 · 10.4 Encryption and Secret Management", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">10.4 Encryption and Secret Management\nAll personally identifiable information (PII) and sensitive data must be encrypted both at\nrest and in transit. Industry-standard algorithms, such as AES-256 for encryption and TLS\n1.2 or higher for data transmission, are required. Secrets, credentials, and keys are securely\nstored and managed using Azure Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, providing restricted access\nand comprehensive auditability.\n\n10.5 Authentication Standards\nAuthentication mechanisms must utilize OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect to ensure secure and\nstandardized user access. Wherever feasible, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is\nrecommended to further enhance security and protect against unauthorized access.\n\n10.6 Supplier Responsibilities\nSuppliers must comply with all defined security and compliance requirements, including the\nintegration of GAS scans into their development workflows. Automated compliance gates\nwithin CI/CD pipelines enforce code quality and security standards, as well as supplier\ncompliance, before any code is merged or deployed.\n\n10.7 Incident Response and Audit Logging\nIncident response procedures are established to enable rapid reaction to security breaches\nor identified vulnerabilities. In addition, comprehensive audit logging is enabled across all\nsystems to provide traceability and support regulatory compliance requirements.\n\n    •  Mandatory use of GitHub Advanced Security for SAST and secret scanning\n    •  DAST performed with OWASP ZAP\n    •  Encryption of all personal/sensitive data (PII)\n    •  Secure secret storage via Azure Vault or AWS Secrets Manager\n    •   Authentication using OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect\n    •  Automated compliance gates in CI/CD pipelines\n    •   Incident response procedures in place\n    •  Audit logging enabled for traceability and compliance<\/div>", "text": "10.4 Encryption and Secret Management\nAll personally identifiable information (PII) and sensitive data must be encrypted both at\nrest and in transit. CI/CD & DevOps", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">11. CI/CD &amp; DevOps\n\n11.1 Introduction to CI/CD &amp; DevOps Tools\nThe selection of CI/CD and DevOps tools is driven by the need for reliability, scalability, and\nefficiency throughout the software delivery lifecycle. Each recommended tool serves a\ndistinct purpose, facilitating automation, infrastructure management, deployment\nconsistency, and operational transparency. The rationale for their adoption centers on\nindustry best practices, cloud-native compatibility, and seamless integration with modern\ndevelopment workflows.\n\nPreference is given to cloud-native and managed services as the primary solution for\ndeploying applications, ensuring optimal integration with cloud platforms, enhanced\nscalability, and streamlined operations. Containers are considered a secondary option and\nare utilized when necessary—such as when a software package is only available as a Docker\nimage, when the application is strategically designed to remain agnostic from any specific\ncloud provider, or when cloud-native services do not meet architectural requirements (for\nexample, code execution reaching serverless timeouts or other limitations). This approach\nensures flexibility while maintaining efficiency and alignment with enterprise goals.\n\n11.2 Detailed Tool Descriptions\n\nGitHub Actions: CI/CD Pipelines\nGitHub Actions streamlines the automation of build, test, and deployment workflows\ndirectly within GitHub repositories. By integrating these processes, GitHub Actions enables\nrapid feedback cycles and the implementation of continuous integration and deployment\npipelines. This automation reduces manual intervention and helps minimize errors during\nthe software delivery process. Additionally, GitHub Actions supports event-driven\nautomation, ensuring that every code change is efficiently validated and deployed.\n\nIt is mandatory for all teams to use the Stellantis GitHub organization and GitHub Actions\nfor CI/CD automation. TeamCity will be made available only for restricted use cases,\nspecifically when a developer can demonstrate that their workflow is not feasible on GitHub\nActions. Requests for TeamCity access must be justified and approved through the\nappropriate channels.\n\nAll other DevOps pipeline tools—including Azure DevOps, AWS Codebuild/pipeline, and any\nsimilar platforms—are strictly prohibited unless an explicit exception is approved. These\ntools are not considered corporate-approved solutions and may not meet necessary\ncompliance or security requirements. Any requests to use alternative DevOps pipelines\nmust undergo a formal approval process and receive documented exception authorization\nbefore implementation.\n\nAll runners must be used solely for pipeline automation tasks and must not be misused as\ngeneral-purpose execution servers, remote desktops, cryptocurrency mining, or for running\nlong-lived background processes unrelated to CI/CD. Misuse of runners can lead to security<\/div>", "text": "11.
