Teams are reminded to\nadhere strictly to these guidelines to ensure operational efficiency and maintain the\nintegrity of the CI/CD environment.\n\nTerraform: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)\nTerraform provides a declarative approach to infrastructure provisioning and management,\nallowing teams to define infrastructure as code. This methodology ensures that\nenvironments are consistent and repeatable across deployments. Terraform’s support for\nversion control of infrastructure changes enhances traceability and control. Its cloud-\nagnostic capabilities enable multi-cloud strategies and automate environment setup,\ncontributing to improved scalability and preparedness for disaster recovery scenarios.\n\nDocker: Containerization\nDocker encapsulates applications and their dependencies into lightweight containers,\npromoting portability and consistency across different environments, including\ndevelopment, testing, and production. This approach streamlines the build process,\naccelerates deployment timelines, and simplifies the scaling of applications. As a result,\ncontainerization using Docker is foundational for adopting cloud-native architectures.\n\nKubernetes (EKS/AKS): Cloud Orchestration\nKubernetes orchestrates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized\nworkloads across clusters. By automating these processes, Kubernetes ensures efficient\noperation of applications at scale. Managed Kubernetes services such as Amazon EKS\n(Elastic Kubernetes Service) and Azure AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) provide robust\nsecurity, high availability, and integrated monitoring, making them suitable for supporting\nenterprise-level cloud operations.\n\n Tool                                  Role\n Github SaaS                              Corporate Codebase\n GitHub Actions                         CI/CD pipelines\n Terraform                                   Infrastructure as Code (IaC)\n Docker                                     Containerization\n Kubernetes (EKS/AKS)                    Cloud orchestration\n\n\n\n11.3 Git-flow &amp; Trunk Best Practices\nChoosing Between Git-flow and Trunk-Based Development\n\nWhen deciding between Git-flow and Trunk-based development, consider the size,\ncomplexity, and criticality of your project. Git-flow is generally recommended for larger,\nmore strategic projects where multiple features, releases, and hotfixes need to be managed\nconcurrently. This workflow provides clear structure for release management, parallel\ndevelopment, and quality assurance, making it ideal for long-term, complex applications\nwith multiple contributors.<\/div>", "text": "vulnerabilities, resource exhaustion, and breaches of compliance. Managed Kubernetes services such as Amazon EKS\n(Elastic Kubernetes Service) and Azure AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) provide robust\nsecurity, high availability, and integrated monitoring, making them suitable for supporting\nenterprise-level cloud operations.\n\n Tool                                  Role\n Github SaaS                              Corporate Codebase\n GitHub Actions                         CI/CD pipelines\n Terraform                                   Infrastructure as Code (IaC)\n Docker                                     Containerization\n Kubernetes (EKS/AKS)                    Cloud orchestration\n\n\n\n11.3 Git-flow & Trunk Best Practices\nChoosing Between Git-flow and Trunk-Based Development\n\nWhen deciding between Git-flow and Trunk-based development, consider the size,\ncomplexity, and criticality of your project. Git-flow is generally recommended for larger,\nmore strategic projects where multiple features, releases, and hotfixes need to be managed\nconcurrently. This workflow provides clear structure for release management, parallel\ndevelopment, and quality assurance, making it ideal for long-term, complex applications\nwith multiple contributors."}, {"id": "d5-s18", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 18 · On the other hand, Trunk-based development is well-suited for proof-of-concept (POC)", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">On the other hand, Trunk-based development is well-suited for proof-of-concept (POC)\nefforts, small teams, or non-strategic projects that require rapid iteration and continuous\nintegration. This approach emphasizes frequent commits to a single branch, encouraging\nfaster feedback and minimizing merge conflicts. For fast-moving, short-lived, or\nexperimental projects, Trunk-based development can accelerate delivery without the\noverhead of managing multiple branches.\n\nIn summary, use Git-flow for projects that demand robust release cycles and strict\nproduction controls, and opt for Trunk-based development when speed and simplicity are\nthe priority, such as in POCs or smaller, less critical initiatives.\n\nGit Flow Best Practices\n\n\n\n\n\nBranching Strategies\nThe Git-flow workflow organizes development into distinct branch types to streamline\nfeature integration, testing, and release management:\n\n    •  Master/Main Branch: Serves as the stable, production-ready branch. Only\n       thoroughly tested and reviewed code is merged here.\n    •  Develop Branch: Aggregates completed features and fixes before release. It acts as\n       the integration branch for ongoing development.\n    •  Feature Branches (feature/*): Isolate new features or enhancements, allowing\n       developers to work independently without impacting the main codebase.\n    •   Release Branches (release/x.y): Prepare for production releases, enabling final\n        testing, bug fixes, and documentation updates before merging to master/main.<\/div>", "text": "On the other hand, Trunk-based development is well-suited for proof-of-concept (POC)\nefforts, small teams, or non-strategic projects that require rapid iteration and continuous\nintegration. This approach emphasizes frequent commits to a single branch, encouraging\nfaster feedback and minimizing merge conflicts. For fast-moving, short-lived, or\nexperimental projects, Trunk-based development can accelerate delivery without the\noverhead of managing multiple branches.\n\nIn summary, use Git-flow for projects that demand robust release cycles and strict\nproduction controls, and opt for Trunk-based development when speed and simplicity are\nthe priority, such as in POCs or smaller, less critical initiatives.\n\nGit Flow Best Practices\n\n\n\n\n\nBranching Strategies\nThe Git-flow workflow organizes development into distinct branch types to streamline\nfeature integration, testing, and release management:\n\n    •  Master/Main Branch: Serves as the stable, production-ready branch. Only\n       thoroughly tested and reviewed code is merged here.\n    •  Develop Branch: Aggregates completed features and fixes before release. It acts as\n       the integration branch for ongoing development.\n    •  Feature Branches (feature/*): Isolate new features or enhancements, allowing\n       developers to work independently without impacting the main codebase.\n    •   Release Branches (release/x.y): Prepare for production releases, enabling final\n        testing, bug fixes, and documentation updates before merging to master/main."}, {"id": "d5-s19", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 19 · •  Hotfix Branches (hotfix/*): Used to quickly address critical production issues.", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">    •  Hotfix Branches (hotfix/*): Used to quickly address critical production issues.\n       Hotfixes branch directly from master/main, are tested and validated rapidly, then\n      merged back into both master/main and develop to keep all branches aligned.\n\nRepository Structure\n    •  Monorepo: Suitable for tightly coupled projects with shared dependencies, enabling\n        unified versioning and streamlined code sharing.\n    •   Multi-repo: Recommended for loosely coupled services, promoting modularity and\n       independent deployment cycles.\n\nWorkflow Recommendations\n    •  Adopt clear naming conventions for branches (e.g., hotfix/ feature/login,\n        release/2.1).\n    •   Regularly synchronize feature branches with develop to minimize merge conflicts.\n    •  Archive stale branches to maintain repository hygiene.\n    •  Automate branch protection rules to enforce review and testing before merging.\n\n\n\nTrunk-Based Development Best Practices\nIt’s important to note that Trunk-Based Development is not the preferred development\napproach for most large-scale or strategic projects. This workflow should be restricted to\nsmall teams, proof of concept (POC) initiatives, or non-strategic projects where rapid\niteration is prioritized over complex release management and governance.\n\nBranching Strategies\nTrunk-Based Development streamlines the software development process by focusing all\nactivity around a single main branch, often referred to as the trunk. This approach\nfacilitates rapid and continuous integration of code changes.\n\nMain/Trunk Branch\nThe main or trunk branch serves as the primary source of truth for the codebase. All\ndevelopers are expected to integrate their changes into this branch frequently, ensuring\nthat it remains in a deployable or nearly deployable state at all times.\n\nShort-Lived Feature Branches\nFeature branches in this workflow should be optional and, when used, are intended for\nsmall, incremental pieces of work. These branches are expected to exist only for a few hours\nto a couple of days before being merged back into the trunk. The practice discourages long-\nlived branches to reduce integration challenges and maintain a smooth workflow.\n\nFeature Flags / Feature Toggles\nTo avoid blocking delivery and allow for uninterrupted integration, incomplete or\nexperimental work can be merged into the trunk behind feature flags or toggles. This<\/div>", "text": "    •  Hotfix Branches (hotfix/*): Used to quickly address critical production issues.\n       Hotfixes branch directly from master/main, are tested and validated rapidly, then\n      merged back into both master/main and develop to keep all branches aligned.\n\nRepository Structure\n    •  Monorepo: Suitable for tightly coupled projects with shared dependencies, enabling\n        unified versioning and streamlined code sharing.\n    •   Multi-repo: Recommended for loosely coupled services, promoting modularity and\n       independent deployment cycles.\n\nWorkflow Recommendations\n    •  Adopt clear naming conventions for branches (e.g., hotfix/ feature/login,\n        release/2.1).\n    •   Regularly synchronize feature branches with develop to minimize merge conflicts.\n    •  Archive stale branches to maintain repository hygiene.\n    •  Automate branch protection rules to enforce review and testing before merging.\n\n\n\nTrunk-Based Development Best Practices\nIt’s important to note that Trunk-Based Development is not the preferred development\napproach for most large-scale or strategic projects. This workflow should be restricted to\nsmall teams, proof of concept (POC) initiatives, or non-strategic projects where rapid\niteration is prioritized over complex release management and governance.\n\nBranching Strategies\nTrunk-Based Development streamlines the software development process by focusing all\nactivity around a single main branch, often referred to as the trunk. This approach\nfacilitates rapid and continuous integration of code changes.\n\nMain/Trunk Branch\nThe main or trunk branch serves as the primary source of truth for the codebase. All\ndevelopers are expected to integrate their changes into this branch frequently, ensuring\nthat it remains in a deployable or nearly deployable state at all times.\n\nShort-Lived Feature Branches\nFeature branches in this workflow should be optional and, when used, are intended for\nsmall, incremental pieces of work. These branches are expected to exist only for a few hours\nto a couple of days before being merged back into the trunk. The practice discourages long-\nlived branches to reduce integration challenges and maintain a smooth workflow.\n\nFeature Flags / Feature Toggles\nTo avoid blocking delivery and allow for uninterrupted integration, incomplete or\nexperimental work can be merged into the trunk behind feature flags or toggles. This"}, {"id": "d5-s20", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 20 · enables ongoing development without the need to wait for a feature’s full completion,", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">enables ongoing development without the need to wait for a feature’s full completion,\nsupporting continuous integration practices.\n\nRepository Structure\nTrunk-Based Development is compatible with both monorepo and multi-repo repository\nstructures.\n\nMonorepo\nA monorepo structure is commonly used with trunk-based development, as it promotes\nconsistency, facilitates the use of shared libraries, supports standardized tooling, and makes\nrefactoring across different components more manageable.\n\nMulti-repo\nAlternatively, this approach is also suitable for multi-repo environments, particularly when\ndeveloping independent microservices. In this scenario, each repository maintains its own\ntrunk branch, which enables isolated deployments and encourages rapid iteration.\n\nWorkflow Recommendations\n    •  Commit and merge changes to the trunk frequently—ideally daily or even more\n      often—to reduce the risk of integration issues.\n    •   Utilize automated continuous integration (CI) pipelines to run tests on every\n      commit before merging changes into the trunk branch.\n    •  Implement feature flags to safely integrate incomplete features without disrupting\n       the main codebase.\n    •  Apply strict code review and quality gates to ensure the stability and integrity of the\n       trunk branch.\n    •  Keep feature branches short-lived and routinely rebase them on the latest version of\n       the trunk.\n    •  Promote automated deployment practices to facilitate continuous delivery and\n       enable rapid releases.\n\n\n\n11.4 Mandatory Code Review Process\nPeer review is essential for maintaining code quality, security, and compliance. All pull\nrequests must undergo mandatory code review by designated peers or tech leads before\nmerging to develop or master/main branches. Automated gates verify code quality, security,\nand supplier compliance.\n\n    •  GitHub Copilot Code Review Assistant: Leverage AI-powered review suggestions to\n        identify potential issues, improve code readability, and ensure adherence to\n       standards. Human reviewers retain final approval authority, ensuring accountability\n      and oversight.\n    •   Linting: Enforce mandatory linting using eslint, pylint, or checkstyle on all code\n       submissions to detect and resolve style and quality violations early in the workflow.<\/div>", "text": "enables ongoing development without the need to wait for a feature’s full completion,\nsupporting continuous integration practices.\n\nRepository Structure\nTrunk-Based Development is compatible with both monorepo and multi-repo repository\nstructures.\n\nMonorepo\nA monorepo structure is commonly used with trunk-based development, as it promotes\nconsistency, facilitates the use of shared libraries, supports standardized tooling, and makes\nrefactoring across different components more manageable.\n\nMulti-repo\nAlternatively, this approach is also suitable for multi-repo environments, particularly when\ndeveloping independent microservices. In this scenario, each repository maintains its own\ntrunk branch, which enables isolated deployments and encourages rapid iteration.\n\nWorkflow Recommendations\n    •  Commit and merge changes to the trunk frequently—ideally daily or even more\n      often—to reduce the risk of integration issues.\n    •   Utilize automated continuous integration (CI) pipelines to run tests on every\n      commit before merging changes into the trunk branch.\n    •  Implement feature flags to safely integrate incomplete features without disrupting\n       the main codebase.\n    •  Apply strict code review and quality gates to ensure the stability and integrity of the\n       trunk branch.\n    •  Keep feature branches short-lived and routinely rebase them on the latest version of\n       the trunk.\n    •  Promote automated deployment practices to facilitate continuous delivery and\n       enable rapid releases.\n\n\n\n11.4 Mandatory Code Review Process\nPeer review is essential for maintaining code quality, security, and compliance. All pull\nrequests must undergo mandatory code review by designated peers or tech leads before\nmerging to develop or master/main branches. Automated gates verify code quality, security,\nand supplier compliance.\n\n    •  GitHub Copilot Code Review Assistant: Leverage AI-powered review suggestions to\n        identify potential issues, improve code readability, and ensure adherence to\n       standards. Human reviewers retain final approval authority, ensuring accountability\n      and oversight.\n    •   Linting: Enforce mandatory linting using eslint, pylint, or checkstyle on all code\n       submissions to detect and resolve style and quality violations early in the workflow."}, {"id": "d5-s21", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 21 · •  Review Roles: Assign peer reviewers for code quality, security leads for", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">    •  Review Roles: Assign peer reviewers for code quality, security leads for\n        vulnerability assessment, and architects for design validation.\n    •  Documentation: Require clear commit messages and update relevant\n       documentation with each change.\n\n11.5 AI-Assisted Coding with GitHub Copilot\n\nUsage Guidelines\nGitHub Copilot is designed to accelerate software development by providing intelligent code\nsuggestions, automating repetitive boilerplate tasks, and delivering context-aware\nrecommendations directly within the integrated development environment (IDE). Its\nintegration into the workflow allows developers to enhance productivity while focusing on\nhigher-level problem solving.\n\nRestrictions on Copilot-Generated Code\nAll code generated by GitHub Copilot must undergo thorough review to ensure correctness,\nsecurity, and compliance with organizational standards. Developers must not use Copilot-\ngenerated code for sensitive logic, proprietary algorithms, or credential management. These\ncritical areas require heightened scrutiny and must never depend solely on AI-generated\ncode to maintain confidentiality and integrity.\n\nBest Practices for Adoption\n    •   Validate all Copilot suggestions against business requirements and established\n        security policies before adoption.\n    •  When Copilot-generated code is integrated, clearly document the rationale for its\n       use within pull request descriptions.\n    •  Leverage Copilot to augment developer expertise, not to replace it. Ultimate\n        accountability and decision-making remain with the developer.\n    •   Disable Copilot when working within highly confidential (e.g C4) or regulated\n       codebases where data privacy is especially critical.\n\nDeveloper Accountability\nDevelopers remain fully responsible for the correctness, security, and maintainability of all\ncode, including contributions assisted by AI tools like GitHub Copilot. Final review and\napproval of code changes are always conducted by human reviewers, ensuring rigorous\noversight and adherence to organizational standards.<\/div>", "text": "    •  Review Roles: Assign peer reviewers for code quality, security leads for\n        vulnerability assessment, and architects for design validation.\n    •  Documentation: Require clear commit messages and update relevant\n       documentation with each change.\n\n11.5 AI-Assisted Coding with GitHub Copilot\n\nUsage Guidelines\nGitHub Copilot is designed to accelerate software development by providing intelligent code\nsuggestions, automating repetitive boilerplate tasks, and delivering context-aware\nrecommendations directly within the integrated development environment (IDE). These\ncritical areas require heightened scrutiny and must never depend solely on AI-generated\ncode to maintain confidentiality and integrity.\n\nBest Practices for Adoption\n    •   Validate all Copilot suggestions against business requirements and established\n        security policies before adoption.\n    •  When Copilot-generated code is integrated, clearly document the rationale for its\n       use within pull request descriptions.\n    •  Leverage Copilot to augment developer expertise, not to replace it. Observability & Logging", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">12. Observability &amp; Logging\nStructured JSON logging is required for all applications to ensure consistent and efficient\nanalysis of system events. Dynatrace will serve as the sole tool for end-to-end observability,\nproviding comprehensive capabilities for monitoring, distributed tracing, anomaly\ndetection, and proactive alerting across the environment. All application monitoring,\ntracing, and analytics will be managed exclusively through Dynatrace, with onboarding and\nintegration procedures detailed in the blueprints to ensure seamless connectivity and\nstandardized dashboards. The Observability Platform Team will maintain and govern\nDynatrace configurations, granting developers access to visualizations, logs, and tracing\ndata relevant to their services.\n\nFor infrastructure logs, collection and forwarding will be handled separately to optimize\ncosts. Logs from cloud environments will be sent directly to the organization&#x27;s SIEM\nsolution using native cloud logging features. For on-premises infrastructure, logs will be\ningested via the Kafka/ELK stack and forwarded to SIEM accordingly.\n\nBlueprints support integrated monitoring and straightforward onboarding, streamlining the\nadoption of Dynatrace and ensuring all development teams have access to the necessary\nobservability tools and processes.\n\n\n13. Documentation &amp; API\nFor effective documentation sharing across our applications, teams should leverage\nConfluence or Microsoft Loop as primary platforms. These tools support collaboration,\nversion control, and accessibility, ensuring all stakeholders are kept informed. To address\nvarying audiences, it is recommended to maintain two distinct documentation spaces: an\n“internal documentation” space focused on technical and operational details for internal\nteams, and an “external documentation” space curated for customers or partners to provide\nuser guides, API usage instructions, and integration information.\n\nWhen documenting APIs, all specifications must reside within our corporate API platform,\nIBM API Connect, which serves as the single source of truth for API lifecycle management.\nBest practices for API documentation include:\n\n    •  Adopting the OpenAPI 3 (Swagger) specification for consistency and compatibility.\n    •   Providing clear examples of request and response payloads.\n    •   Including endpoint descriptions, authentication methods, error codes, and relevant\n        status messages.\n    •   Versioning documentation alongside API releases to ensure alignment and\n        traceability.\n    •   Maintaining up-to-date changelogs and architectural decision records (ADRs) for\n      major design decisions, using provided templates for consistency.<\/div>", "text": "12. Observability & Logging\nStructured JSON logging is required for all applications to ensure consistent and efficient\nanalysis of system events. Dynatrace will serve as the sole tool for end-to-end observability,\nproviding comprehensive capabilities for monitoring, distributed tracing, anomaly\ndetection, and proactive alerting across the environment. All application monitoring,\ntracing, and analytics will be managed exclusively through Dynatrace, with onboarding and\nintegration procedures detailed in the blueprints to ensure seamless connectivity and\nstandardized dashboards. The Observability Platform Team will maintain and govern\nDynatrace configurations, granting developers access to visualizations, logs, and tracing\ndata relevant to their services.\n\nFor infrastructure logs, collection and forwarding will be handled separately to optimize\ncosts. Logs from cloud environments will be sent directly to the organization's SIEM\nsolution using native cloud logging features. For on-premises infrastructure, logs will be\ningested via the Kafka/ELK stack and forwarded to SIEM accordingly.\n\nBlueprints support integrated monitoring and straightforward onboarding, streamlining the\nadoption of Dynatrace and ensuring all development teams have access to the necessary\nobservability tools and processes.\n\n\n13. Documentation & API\nFor effective documentation sharing across our applications, teams should leverage\nConfluence or Microsoft Loop as primary platforms. These tools support collaboration,\nversion control, and accessibility, ensuring all stakeholders are kept informed. To address\nvarying audiences, it is recommended to maintain two distinct documentation spaces: an\n“internal documentation” space focused on technical and operational details for internal\nteams, and an “external documentation” space curated for customers or partners to provide\nuser guides, API usage instructions, and integration information.\n\nWhen documenting APIs, all specifications must reside within our corporate API platform,\nIBM API Connect, which serves as the single source of truth for API lifecycle management.\nBest practices for API documentation include:\n\n    •  Adopting the OpenAPI 3 (Swagger) specification for consistency and compatibility.\n    •   Providing clear examples of request and response payloads.\n    •   Including endpoint descriptions, authentication methods, error codes, and relevant\n        status messages.\n    •   Versioning documentation alongside API releases to ensure alignment and\n        traceability.\n    •   Maintaining up-to-date changelogs and architectural decision records (ADRs) for\n      major design decisions, using provided templates for consistency."}, {"id": "d5-s23", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 23 · Remember, regardless of the documentation platform used for sharing, all API", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">Remember, regardless of the documentation platform used for sharing, all API\ndocumentation must be centrally maintained within IBM API connect to support\ngovernance, discoverability, and compliance with corporate standards.\n\n\n14. Community &amp; Ecosystem\nStellantis encourages open-source contributions, extensibility, and collaboration.\nCommunity forums, regular workshops, and shared repositories promote adoption and\ninnovation. Suppliers are invited to participate in the evolution of standards and feedback\ncycles.<\/div>", "text": "Remember, regardless of the documentation platform used for sharing, all API\ndocumentation must be centrally maintained within IBM API connect to support\ngovernance, discoverability, and compliance with corporate standards.\n\n\n14. "d5-s27", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 27 · A.1.9 Mobile Dart", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">A.1.9 Mobile Dart\n Type               Technology          Standard version     Notes\n                                              guideline\n Language            Dart                  Latest stable with    Use official stable\n                                                Flutter SDK           channel.\n Framework           Flutter                3.27.x                Default for cross-\n                                                                platform mobile\n                                                        (B2E/B2B) apps.\n\nA.1.10 DevOps / IaC (YAML / HCL)\n Type               Technology          Standard version     Notes\n                                              guideline\n Language         YAML / HCL        N/A               Used for\n                                                                     configuration-as-\n                                                                   code.\n Framework          GitHub Actions       Hosted SaaS, rolling   Mandatory CI/CD\n                                                   latest                 orchestration\n                                                                         solution.\n Framework          Terraform             1.10.x               Standard IaC tool\n                                                                        for all clouds.\n\nA.2 JVM and Runtime Version Policy\n\nA.2.1 Java SE / JDK Policy\n    •  Supported JDK distributions are Amazon Corretto (preferred) and community\n      OpenJDK distributions backed by the target cloud or platform.\n    •  The primary Long-Term Support (LTS) baseline is JDK 21 for all new Java projects,\n       unless there is a justified requirement to use JDK 25.\n    •  JDK 25 (LTS) is permitted after validation of build pipelines, frameworks, and\n       runtime images. Migrations from JDK 17 or 21 to JDK 25 follow the standard change\n      management process.\n    •  JDK 17 (LTS) is designated for existing workloads only and must be part of an\n      upgrade plan. No new projects should begin on JDK 17 without a formal exception.\n    •  The minimum JDK for new code is version 17. Java versions lower than 17\n       (including 8 and 11) are strictly prohibited for new developments.\n    •  The bytecode target level must match the selected JDK LTS (e.g., target 21 when\n       building with JDK 21).\n\nA.2.2 Java Application Servers and Containers\n    •  For new developments, prioritize Spring Boot, Quarkus, or serverless/cloud-native\n       runtimes over stand-alone Tomcat, except when there are strong legacy or vendor\n       requirements.\n    •  When a servlet container is required, the default is Embedded Tomcat 11.0.x via\n       Spring Boot.\n    •   Stand-alone Apache Tomcat 11.0.x may be used for specific legacy or vendor cases\n      and must operate on a supported JDK LTS (17/21/25).<\/div>", "text": "A.1.9 Mobile Dart\n Type runtime images. Migrations from JDK 17 or 21 to JDK 25 follow the standard change\n      management process.\n    •  JDK 17 (LTS) is designated for existing workloads only and must be part of an\n      upgrade plan. No new projects should begin on JDK 17 without a formal exception.\n    •  The minimum JDK for new code is version 17. Java versions lower than 17\n       (including 8 and 11) are strictly prohibited for new developments.\n    •  The bytecode target level must match the selected JDK LTS (e.g., target 21 when\n       building with JDK 21).\n\nA.2.2 Java Application Servers and Containers\n    •  For new developments, prioritize Spring Boot, Quarkus, or serverless/cloud-native\n       runtimes over stand-alone Tomcat, except when there are strong legacy or vendor\n       requirements.\n    •  When a servlet container is required, the default is Embedded Tomcat 11.0.x via\n       Spring Boot.\n    •   Stand-alone Apache Tomcat 11.0.x may be used for specific legacy or vendor cases\n      and must operate on a supported JDK LTS (17/21/25)."}, {"id": "d5-s28", "doc": 5, "title": "Page 28 · •  Apache Tomcat 9.0.x is considered maintenance-only for current applications and", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">    •  Apache Tomcat 9.0.x is considered maintenance-only for current applications and\n      must have an established migration plan to Tomcat 11.x.\n\nA.3 Versioning and Upgrade Rules\n    •   All version references in this appendix are guidelines, expressed as major/minor\n       ranges (e.g., 3.5.x, 21.0.x). Teams must pin exact versions in their repositories and\n       lock files.\n    •   Security and bugfix updates within a given major/minor version (e.g., 21.0.7 to\n        21.0.9, 3.5.1 to 3.5.3) are encouraged and do not require exceptions, provided\n      automated tests pass.\n    •  Upgrades to a new major version of any language, framework, JDK, or runtime (e.g.,\n      JDK 21 to 25, Spring Boot 3.x to 4.x) require architectural review and, where\n       necessary, a formal exception or approval process to maintain compatibility and\n       compliance with corporate standards.<\/div>", "text": "    •  Apache Tomcat 9.0.x is considered maintenance-only for current applications and\n      must have an established migration plan to Tomcat 11.x.\n\nA.3 Versioning and Upgrade Rules\n    •   All version references in this appendix are guidelines, expressed as major/minor\n       ranges (e.g., 3.5.x, 21.0.x). Teams must pin exact versions in their repositories and\n       lock files.\n    •   Security and bugfix updates within a given major/minor version (e.g., 21.0.7 to\n        21.0.9, 3.5.1 to 3.5.3) are encouraged and do not require exceptions, provided\n      automated tests pass.\n    •  Upgrades to a new major version of any language, framework, JDK, or runtime (e.g.,\n      JDK 21 to 25, Spring Boot 3.x to 4.x) require architectural review and, where\n       necessary, a formal exception or approval process to maintain compatibility and\n       compliance with corporate standards."}, "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">Introduction\n\nThis document defines the security controls and process requirements for the\nfoundational architecture components and applications (new and existing) deployed\nin public cloud environments. All Stellantis assets hosted and managed in public\nclouds must be in compliance. Broadly speaking, anyone and everyone who is in\nsome way involved for build, configuration and operations of public cloud assets\nshould refer to the stipulations of this document as relevant to their scope of\nresponsibility.\n\nIn order to seek support on any requirements outlined in this document, feel free to\nraise DriveIT ticket (https://fiatchrysler.service-now.com/driveit) for the resolver\ngroup “G_XXX_XXX_CLOUDSECOPS”.\n\n\n\n\n\nCloud Security Control Checklist ver. 1.0                                              Page: 2<\/div>", "text": "Introduction\n\nThis document defines the security controls and process requirements for the\nfoundational architecture components and applications (new and existing) deployed\nin public cloud environments. If you store API keys or any other\n                                         private information in files, keep the files outside your\n                                         application&#x27;s source tree to help ensure your keys or other\n                                         private information do not end up in your source code\n                                       control system. This is particularly important if you use a\n                                      public source code management system such as GitHub.\n 8. Activity      Data access        Ensure that there are no loopholes in the data access\n Audit Logging   logging               security controls and verify this with an audit of who is\n                                    accessing the cloud storage. Must enable data access\n                                       logging if the application is storing protected PII or sensitive\n                                               PII data elements.\n               Tamper proof the    Ensure that the logs are secured in a manner that are\n                  audit logs           protected from being modified and/or deleted.\n 9. Security     Remediations        Application build team must remediate discovered\n Remediations  during build           vulnerabilities and/or misconfigurations before going to\n                                      production.\n                Remediations        Application operation team is responsible for always\n                 during run           maintaining their environment free of security alerts and/or\n                                      misconfigurations during the run phase.\n                Remediation of       Critical and High severity alerts must be promptly\n                     critical and high     remediated at the earliest opportunity. It outlines  the\noverarching principles and minimum control requirements to mitigate risks, ensure compliance\nand promote a culture of Cybersecurity awareness and responsibility among all stakeholders.\n\nDocument administrative control\n\nThe Cybersecurity Program Management Office (PMO) is responsible for the administrative\ncontrol of new and existing Cybersecurity governance documentation. Responsibilities include,\nbut are not limited to, ensuring governance documentation:\n   •   follows the Cybersecurity document control lifecycle process;\n   •   is reviewed at least annually by applicable stakeholders; and\n   •   is communicated to applicable management level stakeholders (N-4)\n\nNote: management  level  stakeholders are  responsible  for communicating  Cybersecurity\ngovernance documentation within their areas of responsibility.\n\nDocument ownership\n\nCybersecurity governance documentation is primarily owned by the CISO with a delegated\nsecondary owner. The CISO and secondary owner are responsible for ensuring that governance\ndocumentation remains technically accurate.\n\nDocument approval\n\nThe CISO has overall approval of Cybersecurity governance documentation but can delegate\naccordingly.\n\nDocument history\n\nPrevious versions of this governance documentation, included tracked changes, can be found in\nthe Cybersecurity Governance Documentation Archive.\n\nVersion control\n\nInitial drafts of this document will be denoted by the format &#x27;0.1&#x27;, indicating preliminary iterations\nsubject to internal review and refinement. Upon approval, documents will transition to official\nstatus, with the initial approved version designated as &#x27;1.00&#x27;. Subsequent revisions shall be\nincrementally numbered to reflect updates, enhancements, or modifications. Version control for\nthis document can be found in Appendix A.\n\nGlossary terms\n\nTerms used within Cybersecurity governance documentation can be found in the Cybersecurity\nGlossary.\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                                Page 2 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\nCybersecurity governance documentation\n\nDocument purpose\n\nThe purpose of Cybersecurity governance documentation is to establish policies, standards,\nprocedures and guidelines  for safeguarding  Stellantis's  information assets. Introduction\n\nOverview\n\n    Currently Stellantis utilizes multiple public cloud services such as Amazon AWS, Microsoft\n   Azure, Google Cloud services and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The security controls and\n    guidelines for governing the usage of public cloud services have evolved separately in each\n    Stellantis region.\n\n\n   This document is intended to provide the administrators, architects, developers, etc., CSP\n    neutral guidance for hosting Stellantis applications and data in a secure and compliant manner\n\n    that is uniform and consistent across all regions.\n\n\nScope\n\n\n   This document provides high-level security controls and guidelines governing the usage, data\n    hosting, and instantiation of Compute assets in public cloud services. The guidance provided\n\n    in this document is agnostic to any Cloud Service Provider.\n\n\nProcess followed to create this Global Cloud Security Control document\n\n  We have reviewed and referred to existing Cloud Security policy documents available within\n    the Stellantis Security Architectural team in North America, xFCA (EMEA) and xPSA (Banque\n\n  PSA Finance) as well AWS/Azure/GCP published controls for creating this converged security\n    control document. We have also referred to the NIST (NIST SP 800-53 Rev.5) and CISA\n   (Cloud Security Technical Reference Architecture v 2.0) as well CIS benchmark guidelines\n\n   (CIS Critical Security Controls version 8.1, CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v5.0.0, CIS\n    Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark v 4.0.0, CIS Control Cloud Companion Guide v8) for\n    best practice and the same is incorporated wherever needed. We have also referred to\n  OWASP Top10 for LLM and Gen AI.\n\n\n   Each security control object specified in this policy document was reviewed, updated, and in\n   accordance with NA, xFCA and xPSA Security Architect team.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                                Page 7 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\nA. Introduction\n\nOverview\n\n    Currently Stellantis utilizes multiple public cloud services such as Amazon AWS, Microsoft\n   Azure, Google Cloud services and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The security controls and\n    guidelines for governing the usage of public cloud services have evolved separately in each\n    Stellantis region.\n\n\n   This document is intended to provide the administrators, architects, developers, etc., CSP\n    neutral guidance for hosting Stellantis applications and data in a secure and compliant manner\n\n    that is uniform and consistent across all regions.\n\n\nScope\n\n\n   This document provides high-level security controls and guidelines governing the usage, data\n    hosting, and instantiation of Compute assets in public cloud services. The guidance provided\n\n    in this document is agnostic to any Cloud Service Provider.\n\n\nProcess followed to create this Global Cloud Security Control document\n\n  We have reviewed and referred to existing Cloud Security policy documents available within\n    the Stellantis Security Architectural team in North America, xFCA (EMEA) and xPSA (Banque\n\n  PSA Finance) as well AWS/Azure/GCP published controls for creating this converged security\n    control document. We have also referred to the NIST (NIST SP 800-53 Rev.5) and CISA\n   (Cloud Security Technical Reference Architecture v 2.0) as well CIS benchmark guidelines\n\n   (CIS Critical Security Controls version 8.1, CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v5.0.0, CIS\n    Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark v 4.0.0, CIS Control Cloud Companion Guide v8) for\n    best practice and the same is incorporated wherever needed. We have also referred to\n  OWASP Top10 for LLM and Gen AI.\n\n\n   Each security control object specified in this policy document was reviewed, updated, and in\n   accordance with NA, xFCA and xPSA Security Architect team.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                                Page 7 of 44"}, {"id": "d7-s9", "doc": 7, "title": "Page 9 · SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n    Controls are designed to be vendor-agnostic, but where specific terminology like ‘Content\n    Delivery Network’ is used in Azure, the same term is retained. Equivalent controls should be\n    applied to corresponding components in other CSPs (e.g., Azure CDN = AWS CloudFront)\n\n\n   For each Cloud Security Control Object, there is a reference number assigned as this will help\n    to refer to the same for assessment/validations for new builds/projects or during audit. SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\nB. General Cloud Security Controls\n\n\n1. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls for IaaS (Infrastructure\nas a Service). Additional  security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the\n\napplication/platform requirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n\n1.1 VM (Virtual Machine)\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n                     Virtual Machine deployments must utilize Stellantis-approved golden\n CS-IS-VM-10   images to ensure compliance with Stellantis security standards and\n                  baseline configurations.\n CS-IS-VM-20   Must ensure that Stellantis owned machine images are not shared publicly.\n CS-IS-VM-30     All virtual machines must be hardened in accordance with CISO-approved\n                   security guidelines to minimize the attack surface. Only essential services\n               and ports required for application functionality shall be enabled.\n\n\n1.2 Network\n\nPlease refer to Network requirement for VM under Network Security domain for VM Network\n\n\n1.3 Access Control\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-AC-10   Temporary escalated privileges (e.g., sudo access in Linux environments)\n               must be granted only to authorized users who require them to perform\n                  occasional privileged tasks. Such access must be time-bound and\n                    auditable.\n CS-IS-AC-20   Must ensure that OS (Operating System) login with 2-step verification on\n                       critical VM is enforced for its access.\n CS-IS-AC-30   Must ensure that privileged access to VM is managed through a corporate\n           PAM solution.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 10 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\nB. Additional  security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the\n\napplication/platform requirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n\n1.1 VM (Virtual Machine)\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n                     Virtual Machine deployments must utilize Stellantis-approved golden\n CS-IS-VM-10   images to ensure compliance with Stellantis security standards and\n                  baseline configurations.\n CS-IS-VM-20   Must ensure that Stellantis owned machine images are not shared publicly.\n CS-IS-VM-30     All virtual machines must be hardened in accordance with CISO-approved\n                   security guidelines to minimize the attack surface. Only essential services\n               and ports required for application functionality shall be enabled.\n\n\n1.2 Network\n\nPlease refer to Network requirement for VM under Network Security domain for VM Network\n\n\n1.3 Access Control\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-AC-10   Temporary escalated privileges (e.g., sudo access in Linux environments)\n               must be granted only to authorized users who require them to perform\n                  occasional privileged tasks. Such access must be time-bound and\n                    auditable.\n CS-IS-AC-20   Must ensure that OS (Operating System) login with 2-step verification on\n                       critical VM is enforced for its access.\n CS-IS-AC-30   Must ensure that privileged access to VM is managed through a corporate\n           PAM solution.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 10 of 44"}, {"id": "d7-s12", "doc": 7, "title": "Page 12 · SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n1.4 Encryption\n\nPlease refer to the Encryption requirement for VM under Encryption domain of VM Encryption\n\n\n1.5 Security Tools\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-TL-10    Must ensure that corporate antimalware solution is deployed in all\n                   instances.\n\n CS-IS-TL-20    Must ensure that a corporate vulnerability assessment solution is deployed\n                     in all instances.\n CS-IS-TL-30    Ensure that Penetration Test and Vulnerability Assessment are performed\n               based on the frequency stipulated in Stellantis Security policy.\n               SSIT-S016 Penetration Testing and Red Team Standard\n\n CS-IS-TL-40    Ensure that a vulnerability scan is performed, and identified vulnerabilities\n                 are remediated for each cloud-deployed service or application after every\n                major change, including configuration or application updates.\n\n\n\n1.6 Patch Management (Security Advisory)\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-PM-10   Ensure that security patches are applied, and software updates are done to\n                 secure the operating system and applications on the virtual machines.\n CS-IS-PM-20   Patches MUST be prioritized based on risk, focusing on vulnerabilities with\n                     significant impact on the organization&#x27;s security posture, especially those\n                   affecting critical systems and high-severity vulnerabilities. Patches MUST\n               comply with the following Service Level Agreements (SLAs) according to\n                      their severity level and timing:\n               Emergency: 48 to 72 hours\n                      Critical: 10 days\n                  High: 30 days\n               Medium: 90 days\n                Low: 180 days or during the next update\n              The mitigation days need to be counted from the date of vulnerability\n                      identified.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 11 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n1.4 Encryption\n\nPlease refer to the Encryption requirement for VM under Encryption domain of VM Encryption\n\n\n1.5 Security Tools\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-PM-10   Ensure that security patches are applied, and software updates are done to\n                 secure the operating system and applications on the virtual machines.\n CS-IS-PM-20   Patches MUST be prioritized based on risk, focusing on vulnerabilities with\n                     significant impact on the organization's security posture, especially those\n                   affecting critical systems and high-severity vulnerabilities. Patches MUST\n               comply with the following Service Level Agreements (SLAs) according to\n                      their severity level and timing:\n               Emergency: 48 to 72 hours\n                      Critical: 10 days\n                  High: 30 days\n               Medium: 90 days\n                Low: 180 days or during the next update\n              The mitigation days need to be counted from the date of vulnerability\n                      identified.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 11 of 44"}, {"id": "d7-s13", "doc": 7, "title": "Page 13 · SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n1.7 Security Hardening\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-SH-10   Must ensure that the IaaS operating system is hardened based on\n               benchmarks published by the Center for Internet Security (CIS).\n CS-IS-SH-20    Ensure that, if, CIS hardening benchmark is not available for any of the\n                 Operating System in cloud environment, then corresponding hardening\n                   guidelines available for on-premises environment is applied.\n CS-IS-SH-30    Ensure that any exceptions to CIS benchmark hardening be clearly\n                documented, and approvals are obtained from the Stellantis CISO team.\n                  Link for Security Exception Request:\n                 Exception requests workflow for applications\n                  Security - How to Create a New Security Exception Request\n\n\n\n2. Network\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls for Network. Additional\n\nsecurity control must be envisaged and enforced based on the application/platform requirements\nand review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n2.1 General\n\n\n Control Ref #                          Security Control Description\n\n CS-NW-GN-10   Must ensure that externally accessible services and applications utilize the\n                   Perimeter (DMZ) network layer, which is secured by a firewall.\n CS-NW-GN-20   Must ensure an Intrusion Prevention System and Intrusion Detection System\n                      to be enabled for all inbound and outbound connections. IPS/IDS capabilities\n                 must handle the requirement of decryption for specific data or applications.\n CS-NW-GN-30   Must ensure that cloud service provider (CSP) network peering mechanisms\n                   are not utilized to establish direct connectivity between the organization’s\n                  cloud-based virtual networks and those of third-party entities\n CS-NW-GN-40   Must ensure that production and non-production workloads are deployed in\n                   separate virtual networks to maintain proper segregation.\n CS-NW-GN-50   Must ensure that a separate Virtual Network subnet is used for each tier of\n                    the application i.e., Web, App, Data tiers.\n CS-NW-GN-60   Must always consider changing the CSP&#x27;s pre-configured set of security rules\n                      to allow minimum port traffic.\n CS-NW-GN-70   Must ensure that control of inbound and outbound network traffic to and from\n                   resources in a virtual network.\n CS-NW-GN-80   Network Security group must allow only the necessary port based on the\n                     application and database requirement.\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 12 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n1.7 Security Hardening\n\n\n Control Ref # STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE", "html": "<div class=\"pdftext\">        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n CS-NW-GN-90   Must ensure that all open network ports are assessed for their relevance and\n                    necessity to the application and promptly closed if found to be unnecessary.\n CS-NW-GN-100  Must ensure that the environment is secured and protected to prevent DDoS\n                    attacks by using CSP supplied native security services.\n CS-NW-GN-110  Must ensure that Content Delivery Network has been used for content\n                       distribution which can prevent direct exposure of the origin server and its\n                  computing components, which results minimal impact in case of DDoS\n                     attack.\n CS-NW-GN-120  Network Security groups must be configured which can act as a firewall for\n                   associated VPC, controlling both inbound and outbound traffic.\n CS-NW-GN-130  Must use either the cloud provider’s private connectivity or customer-owned\n                     private links to connect virtual networks to PaaS services, thereby preventing\n                   data exposure to the public internet.\n CS-NW-GN-140   Public network access to PaaS resources must be disabled wherever\n                   supported by the cloud service provider, to reduce exposure to unauthorized\n                 access and external threats.\n\n\n2.2 Network Firewall\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-NW-FW-10  Must ensure that Hub and spoke topology adhered to simplify the firewall\n                  appliance deployment for centralizing all traffic flowing into the cloud.\n CS-NW-FW-20  Must ensure that Network access control lists (ACLs) are configured which\n               can act as a firewall for associated subnets, controlling both inbound and\n                outbound traffic at the subnet level.\n CS-NW-FW-30  Must ensure that all inbound and outbound exchange flows between Cloud\n               and on-premises network are filtered through a firewall infrastructure\n                   allowing only strictly necessary flows.\n\n\n2.3 WAF (Web Application Firewall)\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-NW-WF-10  External-facing services and applications must be protected by the WAF.\n CS-NW-WF-20 WAF policies must be configured in the mode that actively prevents\n                  malicious traffic from reaching the web application (Prevention/Block).\n CS-NW-WF-30 WAF security service must be configured with V2 or the latest released\n                  version of the WAF security service available and configured with the latest\n                 released version of the rule set/group that corresponds to the OWASP Top\n               10 most common web application attack protections.\n CS-NW-WF-40  Applications handling sensitive data or online transactions must be\n                  protected by a WAF policy that includes Bot protection rules.\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                      Security Control Description\n\n CS-NW-PX-10  Must ensure that Internet requests originating from internal services are\n                  configured to use proxy Virtual Machine\n                 network interfaces must be configured to restrict exposure to the public\n                     internet, ensuring that access is limited to internal or approved secure\n                 networks.\n CS-IS-NW-20   Ensure that all inbound and outbound traffic is filtered through a centralized\n                     firewall that has rules for protecting traffic to the resources.\n CS-IS-NW-30   Ensure that resources not intended for direct internet exposure are\n                deployed within isolated private subnets to enhance security and limit\n                   external access.\n CS-IS-NW-40    All outbound internet traffic originating from internal virtual machines must\n               be routed through an approved proxy service. Direct internet access from\n            VMs is prohibited to ensure traffic inspection, logging, and enforcement of\n                   security policies.\n CS-IS-NW-50   Ensure that RDP/SSH access to VMs is not allowed from the Internet.\n CS-IS-NW-60   Hardened jump server (bastion box) must be used for SSH/RDP connection\n                    to VMs.\n CS-IS-NW-70   Inbound traffic to virtual machines must be restricted to specific IP\n                 addresses, services, and network ports explicitly required for application\n                     functionality. The use of broad port ranges or unrestricted IP access is\n                   prohibited to minimize the attack surface and enforce least privilege network\n                access\n CS-IS-NW-80   Must leverage CSP provided configurations for implementing fine-grained\n                   controls to limit network access to VM.\n\n\nPlease refer to the following for general network security policy requirements:\n\n\nSSIT-S013 NETWORK SECURITY STANDARD\nhttps://docinfogroupe.stellantis.com/ead/doc/ref.00909_23_04243/v.dp/pj\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 14 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n\n2.4 Proxy\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-NW-PX-10  Must ensure that Internet requests originating from internal services are\n                  configured to use proxy services.\n\n\n2.5 VM Network\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-IS-NW-10    Virtual machines must not be assigned public IP addresses. Data Protection\n\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls for Data Protection.\nAdditional security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the application/platform\nrequirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n3.1 General\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-GN-10  Must ensure that encryption key used by the application adheres to relevant\n                   regulatory and legal compliance requirements\n CS-DP-GN-20  Must define TTL (Time-To-Live) for sensitive data cache.\n\n\n3.2 Data Classification\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-DC-10  Must ensure that data is classified by the data / application owner based on\n                  the Stellantis Information Classification Policy C4 Secret, C3 Confidential,\n             C2 Internal and C1 Public. The link for data classification - Information\n                    Classification Annex EN\n\n CS-DP-DC-20  Must enforce cloud service provider’s sensitive data discovery tools as an\n                    additional to ascertain data classification for its security and regulatory\n                  requirements.\n\n\n3.3 Access Control\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-AC-10   Must ensure that access control is configured based on the “least privilege\n                     principle”\n CS-DP-AC-20   Ensure that users having access to a Management Plane/Data Plane (e.g.,\n                    highly privileged user) who has privilege to modify data objects should be\n                   part of “Privilege Activity Monitoring.”\n CS-DP-AC-30   External data sharing for the public or partners who do not have direct\n                access to Stellantis cloud platform must be done through intermediate (jump\n                  servers) servers. Ensure that there is a second layer of controls enforced,\n                such as detective or monitoring controls for this data sharing.\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 15 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n3.                       Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-ST-10   Must ensure that the Storage account is set up to require At-Rest and In-\n                      transit Encryption.\n CS-DP-ST-20   Must ensure the default network access rule for storage accounts is set to\n               be denied.\n CS-DP-ST-30   Must enable &#x27;Storage service encryption&#x27; for blob service on Storage\n                 Accounts.\n CS-DP-ST-40   Must ensure to rotate access keys on Storage Accounts every 90 days or\n                  sooner.\n CS-DP-ST-50   Must enable &#x27;Storage service encryption&#x27; on File Service.\n CS-DP-ST-60   Must configure blob containers where &#x27;Public access level&#x27; is Private.\n CS-DP-ST-70   Must leverage Cloud Provider’s File Storage encryption solution, even if it is\n                  not mandated based on Stellantis “Data Classification”.\n CS-DP-ST-80   Must ensure that Application Architecture using File Storage meets\n                     Stellantis’s Guidelines of Data Protection.\n CS-DP-ST-90   Must ensure and enforce the use of HTTPS when calling the API to access\n                  objects in Storage Accounts.\n CS-DP-ST-100  Must ensure that secure boundaries are created through encryption scope,\n                    for data residing on the same storage account for different applications.\n CS-DP-ST-110  Specific Access configuration for shared storage sets with permissions\n                     tailored to the applications.\n\n\n3.6 Data in Transit\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-DT-10   Must enforce the use of HTTPS when calling the APIs as well REST\n                   API/similar API like gRPC to access objects in Storage Accounts by\n                  enabling native safe file transfer for the Storage Account.\n CS-DP-DT-20   Must ensure that Data Flow is Secure as per Stellantis Data Protection\n                  Guidelines while In-Transit between Cloud Provider&#x27;s Services.\n CS-DP-DT-30   Must ensure that client-side encryption for sensitive data adhered.\n CS-DP-DT-40   Ensure that data tokenized for sensitive data for Confidential and highly\n                    confidential data based on data classification.\n CS-DP-DT-50   Must ensure that Data is Secure as per Stellantis’s Guidelines during Cross-\n                Region Replication.\n CS-DP-DT-60   Whenever the data is exchanged irrespective of confidentiality, we must\n                 ensure a proper encryption of data in transit by encryption in transit features\n               and mechanisms offered by CSP.\n CS-DP-DT-70   Must ensure that to enforce all server-to-server data exchanges are using\n                 secure protocols and services.\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 16 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n3.4 Encryption\nPlease refer Encryption requirement for Data Protection: Data Protection - Encryption\n\n3.5 Storage and Storage Accounts\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-DR-10  Must leverage Cloud Provider’s File Storage encryption solution, even if it is\n                  not mandated based on Stellantis data classification.\n CS-DP-DR-20  Must ensure that Application Architecture using File Storage meets\n                     Stellantis Guidelines of Data Protection.\n CS-DP-DR-30  Must leverage Object Data Storage encryption feature offering from Cloud\n                   Provider, even if the data (per Stellantis’s Data Protection guidelines) is\n               exempted from encryption. This can be achieved through Client-side\n                  encryption or Data Tokenization.\n CS-DP-DR-40   Ensure that Client-side encryption is enforced for Application APIs\n                 performing encryption of sensitive data before storing.\n CS-DP-DR-50  Must ensure that data is protected in test and development environments of\n                   applications through “test data generation” / “data masking.”\n CS-DP-DR-60   Ensure that according to the data Confidentiality, Customer managed keys\n              (CMK) must be used for data encryption.\n\n3.8 Data in Use\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-DP-DU-10  Must monitor direct data manipulation or data definition as well data control\n                    for administrator privileged users based on the Stellantis data classification.\n CS-DP-DU-20   Ensure that there is an assessment performed and prevent whether the\n                 data (based on Stellantis data classification) needs to be cached in a CDN\n                  service or not as the CDN cached data may be available outside an\n                  authorized boundary.\n CS-DP-DU-30  Must ensure that all production data used in pre-production environments\n                 are anonymized or pseudonymized before transferring to the target\n                 environment, using CSPs’ solutions.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 17 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n3.7 Data at Rest\n\n\n\n Control Ref # Cryptography\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls for Cryptography.\n\nAdditional security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the application/platform\nrequirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n\n4.1 General\n\n\n\n Control Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\n CS-CR-GN-10    Must ensure that there is no single encryption key for all data. Must use\n                      different encryption keys based on data or application usage, i.e., internal,\n                     or external customers, etc.\n CS-CR-GN-20    Must ensure periodic rotation of the keys, at least once every 90 days\n                   (about 3 months).\n CS-CR-GN-30    Must ensure that audit logging enabled to track and monitor all access to\n                   encryption keys, ensuring visibility into who accessed them and when.\n CS-CR-GN-40    Must ensure that keys are not used directly, but instead the same should\n                be used through Key IDs through Key Management systems.\n CS-CR-GN-50   To keep track of certificate expirations, we must leverage CSP provided\n                    service for certificate expiration notification.\n CS-CR-GN-60    Must ensure that periodical checks of old and unused keys and remove\n                them if not needed.\n CS-CR-GN-70    Must ensure that periodical review of the user/service access to the keys\n                and remove any unwanted access.\n CS-CR-GN-80    Must ensure that encryption functions mentioned below are used - AES\n                    algorithm (128 bits or higher) TDES/TDEA, RSA (2048 bits or higher),\n             ECC (224 bits or higher), DSA/D-H (2048/224 bits or higher) - AES 256 is\n                      better - data encryption.\n CS-CR-GN-90    Always use a Hardware Security Module/Key Store service to store and\n                      retrieve encryption keys. Consider creating multiple vaults for segregating\n                 access for different users, applications, and environments.\n CS-CR-GN-100   Must use Certificates instead of Keys wherever possible.\n CS-CR-GN-110   Must ensure PKI management policy, including processes for key\n                    generation, distribution, revocation, and expiration are followed.\n CS-CR-GN-120   Must perform audits and reviews of your PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)\n                 system to ensure that it is configured properly and works effectively.\n CS-CR-GN-130   Must use hardware security modules (HSMs) to securely store and\n               manage PKI keys and certificates.\n CS-CR-GN-140   Must ensure that periodic rotation of the private keys is done.\n CS-CR-GN-150   Must ensure that hierarchy of certificates and certificate authority (CA)\n                     levels are used to ensure the integrity and trustworthiness of the PKI\n                  system.\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 18 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n\n\n4.              adhered based on the data confidentiality.\n\n CS-IS-EN-20   Must ensure that implementation of Key validity period and Key rotation\n              schemes in the KMS/HSM as per Container Security\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls for Containers.\nAdditional security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the application/platform\nrequirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n5.1 General\n                                                                                                \nControl run as a non-root user.\nCS-CT-GN-20   Must ensure containers are configured to disallow privilege escalation.\nCS-CT-GN-30  Ensure that the integrity of containers is verified by image signing or\n                   fingerprinting.\nCS-CT-GN-40  Must ensure that only Stellantis approved Container images are used in the\n                environment.\nCS-CT-GN-50  Must ensure that containers operate                         \nControl Ref #                        Security Control Description \n\nCS-CT-RG-10   Must always leverage private registry over public ones.\nCS-CT-RG-20   Must store and                                                                                   \nControl Ref #                        Security Control Description \n\nCS-CT-NW-10   Must protect the resources with class=\"pdftext\">        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n6. Serverless Security\n\n\nThe below mentioned are minimal recommended Cloud Security Controls  for Serverless.\nAdditional security control must be envisaged and enforced based on the application/platform\nrequirements and review of the Cloud Security team.\n\n\n6.1 General\n\n\nControl Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\nCS-SL-GN-10   Must ensure that the latest version of the execution environment is used.\nCS-SL-GN-20   Must ensure that only trusted entities have specific function access.\nCS-SL-GN-30   Ensure that while configuring the function, must determine the smallest set of\n                permissions strictly needed by the function to execute successfully.\nCS-SL-GN-40   Must not use long-lived credentials or hardcoded secrets in functions.\nCS-SL-GN-50   Must ensure that confidential information and credentials are not stored in the\n                  function’s runtime.\nCS-SL-GN-60   Must store environment variables/runtime information with encryption in a\n               secure store.\nCS-SL-GN-70   Must limit access to connected cloud resources and validation of input\n               parameters to secure Serverless functions to prevent injection attacks.\nCS-SL-GN-80   Must ensure that all external libraries and dependencies used by any function\n                are shared with the Security team to analyze and authorize its use.\n\n\n6.2 Network\n\n\nControl Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\nCS-SL-NW-10  Ensure that any external connection must be protected by a web application\n                    firewall.\nCS-SL-NW-20  Ensure that Functions that need access to internal resources must be\n               connected to your VPC.\n\n\n6.3 Encryption\n\n\nControl Ref #                        Security Control Description\n\nCS-SL-EN-10   Must ensure that it always protects the data by leveraging encryption in transit\n               as well at rest.\nCS-SL-EN-20   Ensure that Secrets shall always only exist in memory and must never be\n                logged or written clear text to storage areas.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                              Stellantis classification\n                                  C2 – Internal                               Page 23 of 44<\/div>", "text": "        SSIT-S009-G001 STELLANTIS CLOUD SECURITY CONTROLS GUIDELINE\n\n6.
